questions.question_text: Let $f:ℝ \rightarrow ℝ$ be a differentiable function such that $f(\frac{x+y}{3})=\frac{f(x)+f(y)}{3}$ for all $x,y \in ℝ$ , and $f^{'}(0)=3$ . Then the minimum value of the function $g(x)=3+e^{x}f(x)$ , is:
questions.question_html: Let $f:ℝ \rightarrow ℝ$ be a differentiable function such that $f(\frac{x+y}{3})=\frac{f(x)+f(y)}{3}$ for all $x,y \in ℝ$ , and $f^{'}(0)=3$ . Then the minimum value of the function $g(x)=3+e^{x}f(x)$ , is:
questions.explanation_text: Given $f(\frac{x+y}{3})=\frac{f(x)+f(y)}{3}\text{for all}x,y \in ℝ,$ and $f^{'}(0)=3.$ We have to find the minimum value of $g(x)=3+e^{x}f(x).$ Step 1: Find the form of $f(x)$ We are given a functional equation. We will use it carefully. Let $\frac{x+y}{3}=t.$ Then $x+y=3t.$ The relation becomes $f(t)=\frac{f(x)+f(y)}{3}\text{whenever}x+y=3t.$ We now choose suitable values. Put $x=y=0$ Then $f(0)=\frac{f(0)+f(0)}{3}=\frac{2f(0)}{3}.$ So, $3f(0)=2f(0)⟹f(0)=0.$ Put $y=0$ Then $f(\frac{x}{3})=\frac{f(x)+f(0)}{3}=\frac{f(x)}{3}.$ Thus, $f(x)=3f(\frac{x}{3}).$ Now differentiate both sides with respect to $x$ : $f^{'}(x)=3 \cdot f^{'}(\frac{x}{3}) \cdot \frac{1}{3}=f^{'}(\frac{x}{3}).$ So, $f^{'}(x)=f^{'}(\frac{x}{3}).$ Repeating this, $f^{'}(x)=f^{'}(\frac{x}{3})=f^{'}(\frac{x}{3^{2}})=\cdot s=f^{'}(\frac{x}{3^{n}}).$ As $n \rightarrow \infty$ , $\frac{x}{3^{n}} \rightarrow 0.$ Since $f$ is differentiable, $f^{'}$ is defined at $0$ , so we get $f^{'}(x)=f^{'}(0)=3.$ Hence, $f^{'}(x)=3\text{for all}x.$ Therefore, $f(x)=3x+c.$ But $f(0)=0$ , so $c=0.$ Thus, $f(x)=3x.$ Step 2: Write $g(x)$ Now $g(x)=3+e^{x}f(x)=3+e^{x}(3x)=3+3xe^{x}.$ So, $g(x)=3(1+xe^{x}).$ Step 3: Minimise $xe^{x}$ Let $ℎ(x)=xe^{x}.$ Then $ℎ^{'}(x)=e^{x}+xe^{x}=e^{x}(1+x).$ Since $e^{x}>0$ for all $x$ , we have $ℎ^{'}(x)=0⟺1+x=0⟺x=-1.$ Now, for $x<-1$ , $ℎ^{'}(x)<0$ , so $ℎ$ is decreasing, for $x>-1$ , $ℎ^{'}(x)>0$ , so $ℎ$ is increasing. Hence $ℎ(x)$ has a minimum at $x=-1$ . Its minimum value is $ℎ(-1)=(-1)e^{-1}=-\frac{1}{e}.$ Therefore, $g_{min}=3(1-\frac{1}{e})=3(\frac{e-1}{e}).$ Final Answer $3(\frac{e-1}{e})$ So the correct option is B .
questions.explanation_html:
Given

$f(\frac{x+y}{3})=\frac{f(x)+f(y)}{3}\text{for all}x,y \in ℝ,$

and

$f^{'}(0)=3.$

We have to find the minimum value of

$g(x)=3+e^{x}f(x).$

Step 1: Find the form of $f(x)$

We are given a functional equation. We will use it carefully.

Let

$\frac{x+y}{3}=t.$

Then

$x+y=3t.$

The relation becomes

$f(t)=\frac{f(x)+f(y)}{3}\text{whenever}x+y=3t.$

We now choose suitable values.

Put $x=y=0$

Then

$f(0)=\frac{f(0)+f(0)}{3}=\frac{2f(0)}{3}.$

So,

$3f(0)=2f(0)⟹f(0)=0.$

Put $y=0$

Then

$f(\frac{x}{3})=\frac{f(x)+f(0)}{3}=\frac{f(x)}{3}.$

Thus,

$f(x)=3f(\frac{x}{3}).$

Now differentiate both sides with respect to $x$ :

$f^{'}(x)=3 \cdot f^{'}(\frac{x}{3}) \cdot \frac{1}{3}=f^{'}(\frac{x}{3}).$

So,

$f^{'}(x)=f^{'}(\frac{x}{3}).$

Repeating this,

$f^{'}(x)=f^{'}(\frac{x}{3})=f^{'}(\frac{x}{3^{2}})=\cdot s=f^{'}(\frac{x}{3^{n}}).$

As $n \rightarrow \infty$ ,

$\frac{x}{3^{n}} \rightarrow 0.$

Since $f$ is differentiable, $f^{'}$ is defined at $0$ , so we get

$f^{'}(x)=f^{'}(0)=3.$

Hence,

$f^{'}(x)=3\text{for all}x.$

Therefore,

$f(x)=3x+c.$

But $f(0)=0$ , so

$c=0.$

Thus,

$f(x)=3x.$

Step 2: Write $g(x)$

Now

$g(x)=3+e^{x}f(x)=3+e^{x}(3x)=3+3xe^{x}.$

So,

$g(x)=3(1+xe^{x}).$

Step 3: Minimise $xe^{x}$

Let

$ℎ(x)=xe^{x}.$

Then

$ℎ^{'}(x)=e^{x}+xe^{x}=e^{x}(1+x).$

Since $e^{x}>0$ for all $x$ , we have

$ℎ^{'}(x)=0⟺1+x=0⟺x=-1.$

Now,

  • for $x<-1$ , $ℎ^{'}(x)<0$ , so $ℎ$ is decreasing,

  • for $x>-1$ , $ℎ^{'}(x)>0$ , so $ℎ$ is increasing.

Hence $ℎ(x)$ has a minimum at $x=-1$ .

Its minimum value is

$ℎ(-1)=(-1)e^{-1}=-\frac{1}{e}.$

Therefore,

$g_{min}=3(1-\frac{1}{e})=3(\frac{e-1}{e}).$

Final Answer

$3(\frac{e-1}{e})$

So the correct option is B.

questions.question_html: Let $f(x)$ be a polynomial of degree 5, and have extrema at $x=1$ and $x=-1$ . If $\underset{x \rightarrow 0}{lim}(\frac{f(x)}{x^{3}})=-5$ , then $f(2)-f(-2)$ is equal to:
questions.explanation_text: Given $f(x)$ is a polynomial of degree $5$ Also, $f^{'}(1)=0$ ; $f^{'}(-1)=0$ . Also $\because \underset{x \rightarrow 0}{lim}\frac{f(x)}{x^{3}}=-5$ (fixed and finite) $\therefore f(0)=0$ ; $f^{'}(0)=0$ ; $f^{''}(0)=0$ $\frac{f^{'''}(0)}{6}=-5 \rightarrow f^{'''}(0)=-30$ Hence, let $f^{'}(x)=(ax+b)(x-0)(x-1)(x+1)$ $\rightarrow f^{'}(x)=ax^{4}+bx^{3}-ax^{2}-bx$ $f^{''}(x)=4ax^{3}+3bx^{2}-2ax-b$ $\therefore f^{''}(0)=0 \rightarrow b=0$ $f^{'''}(x)=12ax^{2}+6bx-2a$ $\therefore f^{'''}(0)=-2a=-30$ $\rightarrow a=15$ $\therefore f^{'}(x)=15x.x.(x-1)(x+1)$ $\rightarrow f^{'}(x)=15x^{4}-15x^{2}$ $\rightarrow f(x)=3x^{5}-5x^{3}+C$ $\therefore f(0)=0 \rightarrow C=0$ $\therefore f(x)=3x^{5}-5x^{3}$ $\therefore f(2)-f(-2)=112$
questions.explanation_html:
Given $f(x)$ is a polynomial of degree $5$

Also, $f^{'}(1)=0$ ; $f^{'}(-1)=0$ .

Also $\because \underset{x \rightarrow 0}{lim}\frac{f(x)}{x^{3}}=-5$ (fixed and finite)

$\therefore f(0)=0$ ; $f^{'}(0)=0$ ; $f^{''}(0)=0$

$\frac{f^{'''}(0)}{6}=-5 \rightarrow f^{'''}(0)=-30$

Hence, let

$f^{'}(x)=(ax+b)(x-0)(x-1)(x+1)$

$\rightarrow f^{'}(x)=ax^{4}+bx^{3}-ax^{2}-bx$

$f^{''}(x)=4ax^{3}+3bx^{2}-2ax-b$

$\therefore f^{''}(0)=0 \rightarrow b=0$

$f^{'''}(x)=12ax^{2}+6bx-2a$

$\therefore f^{'''}(0)=-2a=-30$

$\rightarrow a=15$

$\therefore f^{'}(x)=15x.x.(x-1)(x+1)$

$\rightarrow f^{'}(x)=15x^{4}-15x^{2}$

$\rightarrow f(x)=3x^{5}-5x^{3}+C$

$\therefore f(0)=0 \rightarrow C=0$

$\therefore f(x)=3x^{5}-5x^{3}$

$\therefore f(2)-f(-2)=112$

questions.explanation_text: Step 1: Write $f(x)$ without absolute values for different intervals When $x \ge 1$ , $lnx$ is positive and $x-1$ is also positive. So: $f(x)=|lnx|-|x-1|=lnx-(x-1)=lnx-x+1$ for $x \ge 1$ . When $0<x<1$ , $lnx$ is negative and $x-1$ is negative. So: $f(x)=|lnx|-|x-1|=-lnx-(-(x-1))=-lnx+x-1$ for $0<x<1$ . So we can write: $f(x)=⎧⎩⎨\begin{aligned} lnx-x+1 & \text{for}x \ge 1 \\ \\ -lnx+x-1 & \text{for}0<x<1 \end{aligned}$ Step 2: Find the derivative $f^{'}(x)$ in both cases For $x \ge 1,$ $f^{'}(x)=\frac{d}{dx}(lnx-x+1)=\frac{1}{x}-1$ For $0<x<1,$ $f^{'}(x)=\frac{d}{dx}(-lnx+x-1)=-\frac{1}{x}+1$ So, $f^{'}(x)=⎧⎩⎨⎪⎪\begin{aligned} \frac{1}{x}-1 & \text{for}x \ge 1 \\ \\ -\frac{1}{x}+1 & \text{for}0<x<1 \end{aligned}$ Step 3: Check differentiability at $x=1$ From the left of $x=1$ : $f^{'}(1^{-})=-\frac{1}{1}+1=0$ From the right of $x=1$ : $f^{'}(1^{+})=\frac{1}{1}-1=0$ Both one-sided derivatives are equal. So $f(x)$ is differentiable at $x=1$ . Since the formulas for $f^{'}(x)$ are valid everywhere for $x>0$ , $f(x)$ is differentiable for all $x>0$ . Step 4: Check if $f(x)$ is increasing or decreasing For $x>1$ : $f^{'}(x)=\frac{1}{x}-1$ Since $x>1$ , $\frac{1}{x}<1$ . So $f^{'}(x)<0$ , which means $f(x)$ is decreasing for $x>1$ . For $0<x<1$ : $f^{'}(x)=-\frac{1}{x}+1$ Here, $\frac{1}{x}>1$ , so $-\frac{1}{x}+1<0$ , so $f^{'}(x)<0$ . Therefore, $f(x)$ is decreasing for $0<x<1$ also. Step 5: Check the statements (I) $f$ is differentiable at all $x>0$ : True (II) $f$ is increasing in $(0,1)$ : False (III) $f$ is decreasing in $(1,\infty)$ : True So only statements (I) and (III) are correct.

questions.explanation_text: Equation of the Normal to the Parabola: The equation for the normal to the parabola $y^{2}=8x$ can be expressed as: $y=mx-2am-am^{3}\text{where}a=2$ Simplifying, we have: $y=mx-4m-2m^{3}$ Center and Radius of the Circle: The given second equation $x^{2}+y^{2}+12y+35=0$ can be rewritten to find the center and radius of the circle: Rewrite it as $x^{2}+(y+6)^{2}=1$ . Thus, the center of the circle is $C(0,-6)$ and the radius $r=1$ . Finding the Slope of the Normal: To find the point $P$ on the parabola where the normal meets, equate: $-6=-4m-2m^{3}$ Solving for $m$ gives: $m=1$ Determine Point $P$ on the Parabola: Substituting $m=1$ back to find $P(am^{2},-2am)$ : $P(2,-4)$ Calculate the Shortest Distance: The shortest distance from point $P(2,-4)$ to the center $C(0,-6)$ minus the radius is: $CP-r=\sqrt{(2-0)^{2}+(-4+6)^{2}}-1=\sqrt{4+4}-1$ $=\sqrt{8}-1=2\sqrt{2}-1$ Thus, the shortest distance between the given curves is $2\sqrt{2}-1$ .
questions.explanation_html:
Equation of the Normal to the Parabola:

The equation for the normal to the parabola $y^{2}=8x$ can be expressed as:

$y=mx-2am-am^{3}\text{where}a=2$

Simplifying, we have:

$y=mx-4m-2m^{3}$

Center and Radius of the Circle:

The given second equation $x^{2}+y^{2}+12y+35=0$ can be rewritten to find the center and radius of the circle:

Rewrite it as $x^{2}+(y+6)^{2}=1$ .

Thus, the center of the circle is $C(0,-6)$ and the radius $r=1$ .

Finding the Slope of the Normal:

To find the point $P$ on the parabola where the normal meets, equate:

$-6=-4m-2m^{3}$

Solving for $m$ gives:

$m=1$

Determine Point $P$ on the Parabola:

Substituting $m=1$ back to find $P(am^{2},-2am)$ :

$P(2,-4)$

Calculate the Shortest Distance:

The shortest distance from point $P(2,-4)$ to the center $C(0,-6)$ minus the radius is:

$CP-r=\sqrt{(2-0)^{2}+(-4+6)^{2}}-1=\sqrt{4+4}-1$

$=\sqrt{8}-1=2\sqrt{2}-1$

Thus, the shortest distance between the given curves is $2\sqrt{2}-1$ .

questions.explanation_text: To determine the value of $f(3)$ for the function $f(x)=2x^{3}-9ax^{2}+12a^{2}x+1$ , where $a>0$ , we follow these steps: First, find the critical points by setting the derivative equal to zero: $f^{'}(x)=6x^{2}-18ax+12a^{2}=0$ Factoring gives: $6(x-a)(x-2a)=0$ Thus, the critical points are $x=a$ and $x=2a$ . $x=a$ corresponds to a local maximum. $x=2a$ corresponds to a local minimum. According to the problem, $p^{2}=q$ . Substituting $p=a$ and $q=2a$ gives: $a^{2}=2a$ Solving for $a$ gives: $a(a-2)=0$ Since $a>0$ , we have $a=2$ . Now, substitute $a=2$ back into the function: $f(x)=2x^{3}-18x^{2}+48x+1$ To find $f(3)$ : $f(3)=2(3)^{3}-18(3)^{2}+48(3)+1$ Calculate each term: $2(3)^{3}=54$ $18(3)^{2}=162$ $48(3)=144$ Thus, $f(3)=54-162+144+1=37$ So, $f(3)=37$ .

$f^{'}(x)=6x^{2}-18ax+12a^{2}=0$

Factoring gives:

$6(x-a)(x-2a)=0$

Thus, the critical points are $x=a$ and $x=2a$ .

$x=a$ corresponds to a local maximum.

$x=2a$ corresponds to a local minimum.

According to the problem, $p^{2}=q$ . Substituting $p=a$ and $q=2a$ gives:

$f(x)=2x^{3}-18x^{2}+48x+1$

To find $f(3)$ :

$f(3)=2(3)^{3}-18(3)^{2}+48(3)+1$

Calculate each term:

$2(3)^{3}=54$

$18(3)^{2}=162$

$48(3)=144$

Thus,

$f(3)=54-162+144+1=37$

So, $f(3)=37$ .

questions.explanation_text: We are given $f(x)=\int_{0}^{x^{2}}\frac{t^{2}-8t+15}{e^{t}}dt,x \in ℝ.$ To find the local extrema, we first compute the derivative using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus and the chain rule. Step 1. Rewrite the derivative: Let $F(u)=\int_{0}^{u}\frac{t^{2}-8t+15}{e^{t}}dt,$ so that $f(x)=F(x^{2}).$ Then by the chain rule, $f^{'}(x)=F^{'}(x^{2}) \cdot 2x.$ Since $F^{'}(u)=\frac{u^{2}-8u+15}{e^{u}},$ we substitute $u=x^{2}$ to get $f^{'}(x)=\frac{(x^{2})^{2}-8x^{2}+15}{e^{x^{2}}} \cdot 2x=\frac{2x(x^{4}-8x^{2}+15)}{e^{x^{2}}}.$ Step 2. Factor and Identify Critical Points: Factor the polynomial $x^{4}-8x^{2}+15$ by writing it in terms of $x^{2}$ . Let $y=x^{2}$ , then $y^{2}-8y+15=(y-3)(y-5)$ so that $x^{4}-8x^{2}+15=(x^{2}-3)(x^{2}-5).$ Thus, $f^{'}(x)=\frac{2x(x^{2}-3)(x^{2}-5)}{e^{x^{2}}}.$ Since $e^{x^{2}}>0$ for all $x$ , the zeros of $f^{'}(x)$ are determined by $2x(x^{2}-3)(x^{2}-5)=0.$ That gives the critical points: $2x=0 \Rightarrow x=0$ , $x^{2}-3=0 \Rightarrow x= \pm \sqrt{3}$ , $x^{2}-5=0 \Rightarrow x= \pm \sqrt{5}$ . Step 3. Analyzing the Sign of $f^{'}(x)$ : We need to determine the nature (maximum or minimum) by looking at the sign changes of $f^{'}(x)$ on the intervals determined by the critical points $x=-\sqrt{5}$ , $x=-\sqrt{3}$ , $x=0$ , $x=\sqrt{3}$ , and $x=\sqrt{5}$ . Notice that the factor $2x(x^{2}-3)(x^{2}-5)$ will dictate the sign. Let’s define: $ℎ(x)=x(x^{2}-3)(x^{2}-5).$ Examine the sign of $ℎ(x)$ in each interval: For $x<-\sqrt{5}$ : $x$ is negative. $x^{2}>5$ so $x^{2}-3>0$ and $x^{2}-5>0$ . Product: negative $\times$ positive $\times$ positive = negative. Thus, $f^{'}(x)<0$ . For $-\sqrt{5}<x<-\sqrt{3}$ : $x$ is negative. $x^{2}$ is between 3 and 5 so $x^{2}-3>0$ while $x^{2}-5<0$ . Product: negative $\times$ positive $\times$ negative = positive. Thus, $f^{'}(x)>0$ . For $-\sqrt{3}<x<0$ : $x$ is negative. $x^{2}<3$ so both $x^{2}-3<0$ and $x^{2}-5<0$ . Product: negative $\times$ negative $\times$ negative = negative. Thus, $f^{'}(x)<0$ . For $0<x<\sqrt{3}$ : $x$ is positive. $x^{2}<3$ so both $x^{2}-3<0$ and $x^{2}-5<0$ . Product: positive $\times$ negative $\times$ negative = positive. Thus, $f^{'}(x)>0$ . For $\sqrt{3}<x<\sqrt{5}$ : $x$ is positive. $x^{2}$ is between 3 and 5 so $x^{2}-3>0$ while $x^{2}-5<0$ . Product: positive $\times$ positive $\times$ negative = negative. Thus, $f^{'}(x)<0$ . For $x>\sqrt{5}$ : $x$ is positive. $x^{2}>5$ so both $x^{2}-3>0$ and $x^{2}-5>0$ . Product: positive $\times$ positive $\times$ positive = positive. Thus, $f^{'}(x)>0$ . Step 4. Classify the Critical Points: At $x=-\sqrt{5}$ : $f^{'}(x)$ changes from negative to positive → local minimum. At $x=-\sqrt{3}$ : $f^{'}(x)$ changes from positive to negative → local maximum. At $x=0$ : $f^{'}(x)$ changes from negative to positive → local minimum. At $x=\sqrt{3}$ : $f^{'}(x)$ changes from positive to negative → local maximum. At $x=\sqrt{5}$ : $f^{'}(x)$ changes from negative to positive → local minimum. Step 5. Conclusion: There are local maximum points at $x=-\sqrt{3}$ and $x=\sqrt{3}$ (2 points in total), and local minimum points at $x=-\sqrt{5}$ , $x=0$ , and $x=\sqrt{5}$ (3 points in total). Thus, the numbers of local maximum and local minimum points of $f$ are 2 and 3, respectively. The correct option is Option C.

Product: negative $\times$ negative $\times$ negative = negative.

Thus, $f^{'}(x)<0$ .

For $0<x<\sqrt{3}$ :

$x$ is positive.

Product: positive $\times$ negative $\times$ negative = positive.

Thus, $f^{'}(x)>0$ .

For $\sqrt{3}<x<\sqrt{5}$ :

$x^{2}$ is between 3 and 5 so $x^{2}-3>0$ while $x^{2}-5<0$ .

Product: positive $\times$ positive $\times$ negative = negative.

Thus, $f^{'}(x)<0$ .

For $x>\sqrt{5}$ :

$x$ is positive.

$x^{2}>5$ so both $x^{2}-3>0$ and $x^{2}-5>0$ .

questions.explanation_text: To find the number of critical points of the function $f(x)=(x-2)^{2/3}(2x+1)$ , we need to determine where its derivative $f^{'}(x)$ is equal to zero or undefined. Critical points occur where the derivative is zero or does not exist. First, let's find the derivative of the function: $f(x)=(x-2)^{2/3}(2x+1)$ We apply the product rule for differentiation, which states that $(uv)^{'}=u^{'}v+uv^{'}$ , where $u=(x-2)^{2/3}$ and $v=2x+1$ . We need the derivatives of $u$ and $v$ : For $u=(x-2)^{2/3}$ , we use the chain rule: $u^{'}(x)=\frac{d}{dx}[(x-2)^{2/3}]=\frac{2}{3}(x-2)^{-1/3} \cdot 1=\frac{2}{3}(x-2)^{-1/3}$ The derivative of $v$ is straightforward, as $v=2x+1$ : $v^{'}(x)=2$ Now we apply the product rule: $f^{'}(x)=u^{'}(x)v(x)+u(x)v^{'}(x)$ Substituting $u$ , $u^{'}$ , and $v$ , we get: $f^{'}(x)=(\frac{2}{3}(x-2)^{-1/3})(2x+1)+((x-2)^{2/3})(2)$ This simplifies to: $f^{'}(x)=\frac{2(2x+1)}{3(x-2)^{1/3}}+2(x-2)^{2/3}$ For critical points, we need to solve $f^{'}(x)=0$ or where it is undefined. 1. Solve for where the derivative is zero: $\frac{2(2x+1)}{3(x-2)^{1/3}}+2(x-2)^{2/3}=0$ Combining like terms in a common denominator, we get: $\frac{2(2x+1)+6(x-2)}{3(x-2)^{1/3}}=0$ Simplifying the numerator: $2(2x+1)+6(x-2)=4x+2+6x-12=10x-10=10(x-1)$ So: $\frac{10(x-1)}{3(x-2)^{1/3}}=0$ The numerator is zero when: $10(x-1)=0$ Therefore: $x=1$ 2. Solve for where the derivative is undefined: The denominator, $3(x-2)^{1/3}$ , is undefined when $(x-2)^{1/3}=0$ , which happens at: $x=2$ From the above analysis, the critical points are at $x=1$ and $x=2$ . Thus, there are 2 critical points. Therefore, the number of critical points of the function $f(x)=(x-2)^{2/3}(2x+1)$ is: Option A
questions.explanation_html:
To find the number of critical points of the function $f(x)=(x-2)^{2/3}(2x+1)$ , we need to determine where its derivative $f^{'}(x)$ is equal to zero or undefined. Critical points occur where the derivative is zero or does not exist.

First, let's find the derivative of the function:

$f(x)=(x-2)^{2/3}(2x+1)$

We apply the product rule for differentiation, which states that $(uv)^{'}=u^{'}v+uv^{'}$ , where $u=(x-2)^{2/3}$ and $v=2x+1$ .

We need the derivatives of $u$ and $v$ :

For $u=(x-2)^{2/3}$ , we use the chain rule:

$u^{'}(x)=\frac{d}{dx}[(x-2)^{2/3}]=\frac{2}{3}(x-2)^{-1/3} \cdot 1=\frac{2}{3}(x-2)^{-1/3}$

The derivative of $v$ is straightforward, as $v=2x+1$ :

$v^{'}(x)=2$

Now we apply the product rule:

$f^{'}(x)=u^{'}(x)v(x)+u(x)v^{'}(x)$

Substituting $u$ , $u^{'}$ , and $v$ , we get:

$f^{'}(x)=(\frac{2}{3}(x-2)^{-1/3})(2x+1)+((x-2)^{2/3})(2)$

This simplifies to:

$f^{'}(x)=\frac{2(2x+1)}{3(x-2)^{1/3}}+2(x-2)^{2/3}$

For critical points, we need to solve $f^{'}(x)=0$ or where it is undefined.

1. Solve for where the derivative is zero:

$\frac{2(2x+1)}{3(x-2)^{1/3}}+2(x-2)^{2/3}=0$

Combining like terms in a common denominator, we get:

$\frac{2(2x+1)+6(x-2)}{3(x-2)^{1/3}}=0$

Simplifying the numerator:

$2(2x+1)+6(x-2)=4x+2+6x-12=10x-10=10(x-1)$

So:

$\frac{10(x-1)}{3(x-2)^{1/3}}=0$

The numerator is zero when:

$10(x-1)=0$

Therefore:

$x=1$

2. Solve for where the derivative is undefined:

The denominator, $3(x-2)^{1/3}$ , is undefined when $(x-2)^{1/3}=0$ , which happens at:

$x=2$

From the above analysis, the critical points are at $x=1$ and $x=2$ . Thus, there are 2 critical points.

Therefore, the number of critical points of the function $f(x)=(x-2)^{2/3}(2x+1)$ is:

Option A

questions.explanation_text: Let's analyze the function $f(x)=(cosx)-x+1$ over the interval $[0,\pi]$ and the statements provided. First, let's consider statement (S1): (S1) $f(x)=0$ for only one value of $x$ in $[0,\pi]$ . To examine this statement, we need to explore the zeros of the function $f(x)$ within the given interval. Let's define and analyze the function: $f(x)=cosx-x+1$ We seek to determine if $f(x)=0$ has only one solution in the interval $[0,\pi]$ . To do this, we can use the Intermediate Value Theorem and the behavior of the function's derivative. First, compute the derivative of $f(x)$ : $f^{'}(x)=\frac{d}{dx}(cosx-x+1)=-sinx-1$ The critical points occur when $f^{'}(x)=0$ : $-sinx-1=0 \Rightarrow sinx=-1$ . The equation $sinx=-1$ does not hold for any $x$ in $[0,\pi]$ . Note that: For $x \in [0,\frac{\pi}{2}]$ , $sinx$ ranges from 0 to 1. For $x \in [\frac{\pi}{2},\pi]$ , $sinx$ ranges from 1 to 0. Since $f^{'}(x)$ is always negative (i.e., $f^{'}(x)<0$ ), $f(x)$ is a strictly decreasing function in $[0,\pi]$ . Moreover, we evaluate: $f(0)=cos0-0+1=1+1=2$ $f(\pi)=cos\pi-\pi+1=-1-\pi+1=-\pi$ Given the continuous and strictly decreasing nature of $f(x)$ in $[0,\pi]$ , by the Intermediate Value Theorem, there is exactly one value of $x$ in the interval $[0,\pi]$ where $f(x)=0$ , confirming (S1). Now, let's consider statement (S2): (S2) $f(x)$ is decreasing in $[0,\frac{\pi}{2}]$ and increasing in $[\frac{\pi}{2},\pi]$ . We already analyzed that $f^{'}(x)$ shows that $f^{'}(x)=-sinx-1$ is always less than zero in $[0,\pi]$ . No interval exists where the derivative is positive. This means that $f(x)$ is strictly decreasing throughout the entire interval of $[0,\pi]$ , invalidating (S2). Therefore, the correct option is: Option B : Only (S1) is correct.

questions.explanation_text:
Given the function: $f(x)=x-2sinxcosx+\frac{1}{3}sin3x$ We want to find the maximum value of this expression for $0 \le x \le \pi$ . Step 1: Rewrite the expression Notice that we can rewrite the expression as: $f(x)=x-sin2x+\frac{1}{3}sin3x$ Step 2: Find the first derivative Now, let's find the derivative of this expression with respect to $x$ : $f^{'}(x)=1-2cos2x+cos3x$ Step 3: Find the critical points To find the critical points, we set $f^{'}(x)=0$ : $1-2cos2x+cos3x=0$ Step 4: Solve for x This equation can be rewritten as: $(2cosx+\sqrt{3})(2cosx-\sqrt{3})(cosx-1)=0$ We get three possible solutions for $x$ : $cosx=\frac{-\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},1$ Which gives us: $x=\frac{5\pi}{6},\frac{\pi}{6},0$ Step 5: Find the second derivative Now, let's find the second derivative of the expression: $f^{''}(x)=4sin2x-3sin3x$ Step 6: Analyze the critical points
Evaluate the second derivative at the critical points: $f^{''}(\frac{5\pi}{6})=-2\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{3}<0$ , indicating a local maximum. $f^{''}(\frac{\pi}{6})=2\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{3}>0$ , indicating a local minimum. $f^{''}(0)=0$ , inconclusive. Step 7: Evaluate the function at the local maximum point and the boundary points
Since we are looking for the maximum value of $f(x)$ , we can now evaluate the function at the local maximum point and the boundary points: $f(\frac{5\pi}{6})=\frac{5\pi}{6}+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}+\frac{1}{3}=\frac{5\pi+2+3\sqrt{3}}{6}$ $f(0)=0$ $f(\pi)=\pi$ Step 8: Compare the values
The maximum value of $f(x)$ is given by $f(\frac{5\pi}{6})=\frac{5\pi+2+3\sqrt{3}}{6}$ .
questions.explanation_html:
Given the function:

$f(x)=x-2sinxcosx+\frac{1}{3}sin3x$

We want to find the maximum value of this expression for $0 \le x \le \pi$ .

Step 1: Rewrite the expression

Notice that we can rewrite the expression as:

$f(x)=x-sin2x+\frac{1}{3}sin3x$

Step 2: Find the first derivative

Now, let's find the derivative of this expression with respect to $x$ :

$f^{'}(x)=1-2cos2x+cos3x$

Step 3: Find the critical points

To find the critical points, we set $f^{'}(x)=0$ :

$1-2cos2x+cos3x=0$

Step 4: Solve for x

This equation can be rewritten as:

$(2cosx+\sqrt{3})(2cosx-\sqrt{3})(cosx-1)=0$

We get three possible solutions for $x$ :

$cosx=\frac{-\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},1$

Which gives us: $x=\frac{5\pi}{6},\frac{\pi}{6},0$

Step 5: Find the second derivative

Now, let's find the second derivative of the expression:

$f^{''}(x)=4sin2x-3sin3x$

Step 6: Analyze the critical points Evaluate the second derivative at the critical points:

  1. $f^{''}(\frac{5\pi}{6})=-2\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{3}<0$ , indicating a local maximum.
  2. $f^{''}(\frac{\pi}{6})=2\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{3}>0$ , indicating a local minimum.
  3. $f^{''}(0)=0$ , inconclusive.

Step 7: Evaluate the function at the local maximum point and the boundary points Since we are looking for the maximum value of $f(x)$ , we can now evaluate the function at the local maximum point and the boundary points:

  1. $f(\frac{5\pi}{6})=\frac{5\pi}{6}+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}+\frac{1}{3}=\frac{5\pi+2+3\sqrt{3}}{6}$
  2. $f(0)=0$
  3. $f(\pi)=\pi$

Step 8: Compare the values The maximum value of $f(x)$ is given by $f(\frac{5\pi}{6})=\frac{5\pi+2+3\sqrt{3}}{6}$ .

questions.explanation_text: Let the slope of tangent at any point $(x,y)$ on a curve $y=y(x)$ is $\frac{dy}{dx}$ According to the question, $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x^{2}+y^{2}}{2xy}(x>0)$ [Given] $\begin{aligned} & \text{Let}y=vx \Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}=v+x\frac{dv}{dx} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow v+x\frac{dv}{dx}=\frac{x^{2}+v^{2}x^{2}}{2vx^{2}}=\frac{1+v^{2}}{2v} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x\frac{dv}{dx}=\frac{1+v^{2}}{2v}-v=\frac{1-v^{2}}{2v} \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \int \frac{2vdv}{1-v^{2}}=\int \frac{dx}{x}\text{[Taking integration on both sides]} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow -ln|1-v^{2}|=lnx-lnc \\ \\ & \Rightarrow ln(1-v^{2})x=lnc(c=\text{constant}) \\ \\ & \Rightarrow (1-y^{2}/x^{2}) \cdot x=c \\ \\ & \Rightarrow (x^{2}-y^{2})=cx \end{aligned}$ Put $y(2)=0 \Rightarrow c=2$ $\begin{aligned} & \therefore x^{2}-y^{2}=2x \\ \\ & \therefore y^{2}=x^{2}-2x \\ \\ & \Rightarrow y(x)= \pm \sqrt{x^{2}-2x} \end{aligned}$ Put $x=8$ , we get $\Rightarrow y(8)= \pm \sqrt{64-16}= \pm \sqrt{48}= \pm 4\sqrt{3}$
questions.explanation_html:
Let the slope of tangent at any point

$(x,y)$ on a curve $y=y(x)$ is $\frac{dy}{dx}$

According to the question, $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x^{2}+y^{2}}{2xy}(x>0)$ [Given]

$\begin{aligned} & \text{Let}y=vx \Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}=v+x\frac{dv}{dx} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow v+x\frac{dv}{dx}=\frac{x^{2}+v^{2}x^{2}}{2vx^{2}}=\frac{1+v^{2}}{2v} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x\frac{dv}{dx}=\frac{1+v^{2}}{2v}-v=\frac{1-v^{2}}{2v} \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \int \frac{2vdv}{1-v^{2}}=\int \frac{dx}{x}\text{[Taking integration on both sides]} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow -ln|1-v^{2}|=lnx-lnc \\ \\ & \Rightarrow ln(1-v^{2})x=lnc(c=\text{constant}) \\ \\ & \Rightarrow (1-y^{2}/x^{2}) \cdot x=c \\ \\ & \Rightarrow (x^{2}-y^{2})=cx \end{aligned}$

Put $y(2)=0 \Rightarrow c=2$

$\begin{aligned} & \therefore x^{2}-y^{2}=2x \\ \\ & \therefore y^{2}=x^{2}-2x \\ \\ & \Rightarrow y(x)= \pm \sqrt{x^{2}-2x} \end{aligned}$

Put $x=8$ , we get

$\Rightarrow y(8)= \pm \sqrt{64-16}= \pm \sqrt{48}= \pm 4\sqrt{3}$

questions.explanation_text: $\text{Let}y=(\frac{\sqrt{3e}}{2sinx})^{sin^{2}x}$ $lny=sin^{2}x \cdot ln(\frac{\sqrt{3e}}{2sinx})$ $\frac{1}{y}y^{'}=ln(\frac{\sqrt{3e}}{2sinx})2sinxcosx+sin^{2}x\frac{2sinx}{\sqrt{3e}}\frac{\sqrt{3e}}{2}(-cosecxcotx)$ For maxima or minima, $\frac{dy}{dx}=0$ $\Rightarrow ln(\frac{\sqrt{3e}}{2sinx})2sinxcosx-sinxcosx=0$ $\Rightarrow sinxcosx[2ln(\frac{\sqrt{3e}}{2sinx})-1]=0$ $\Rightarrow ln(\frac{3e}{4sin^{2}x})=1$ $\Rightarrow \frac{3e}{4sin^{2}x}=e$ $\Rightarrow sin^{2}x=\frac{3}{4}$ $\Rightarrow sinx=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}(\text{as}x \in (0,\frac{\pi}{2}))$ $\Rightarrow \text{Local max value}=(\frac{\sqrt{3e}}{\sqrt{3}})^{3/4}=e^{3/8}=\frac{k}{e}$ $\Rightarrow k^{8}=e^{11}$ $\therefore$ $(\frac{k}{e})^{8}+\frac{k^{8}}{e^{5}}+k^{8}=e^{3}+e^{6}+e^{11}$

$\text{Let}y=(\frac{\sqrt{3e}}{2sinx})^{sin^{2}x}$

$lny=sin^{2}x \cdot ln(\frac{\sqrt{3e}}{2sinx})$

$\frac{1}{y}y^{'}=ln(\frac{\sqrt{3e}}{2sinx})2sinxcosx+sin^{2}x\frac{2sinx}{\sqrt{3e}}\frac{\sqrt{3e}}{2}(-cosecxcotx)$

For maxima or minima, $\frac{dy}{dx}=0$

$\Rightarrow ln(\frac{\sqrt{3e}}{2sinx})2sinxcosx-sinxcosx=0$

$\Rightarrow sinxcosx[2ln(\frac{\sqrt{3e}}{2sinx})-1]=0$

$\Rightarrow ln(\frac{3e}{4sin^{2}x})=1$

$\Rightarrow \frac{3e}{4sin^{2}x}=e$

$\Rightarrow sin^{2}x=\frac{3}{4}$

$\Rightarrow sinx=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}(\text{as}x \in (0,\frac{\pi}{2}))$

$\Rightarrow \text{Local max value}=(\frac{\sqrt{3e}}{\sqrt{3}})^{3/4}=e^{3/8}=\frac{k}{e}$

$\Rightarrow k^{8}=e^{11}$

$\therefore$ $(\frac{k}{e})^{8}+\frac{k^{8}}{e^{5}}+k^{8}=e^{3}+e^{6}+e^{11}$

questions.question_html: A square piece of tin of side 30 cm is to be made into a box without top by cutting a square from each corner and folding up the flaps to form a box. If the volume of the box is maximum, then its surface area (in cm $^{2}$ ) is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Given, length of square sheet of side is $30cm$ . Let, side of small square be $xcm$ . Since, a square piece of tin is to be made into a box without top by cutting square from each corner and folding up the flaps to from a box. Then, this shape formed a cuboidal shape. Thus, volume of the box $(V)$ $\begin{aligned} & =(30-2x)(30-2x)x \\ \\ & \Rightarrow V=x(30-2x)^{2} \end{aligned}$ On differentiating both side with respect to $x$ , we get $\begin{aligned} \frac{dV}{dx} & =(30-2x)^{2}+x{2(30-2x) \cdot (-2)} \\ \\ & =(30-2x)^{2}-4x(30-2x) \\ \\ & =(30-2x){30-6x} \end{aligned}$ Therefore, maximum of $V,\frac{dV}{dx}=0$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow (30-2x)(30-6x)=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x=15\text{or}x=5[x=15\text{(not taken)}] \end{aligned}$ Thus, $x=5$ So, the surface area $\begin{aligned} =4 \times (30-2x) \times x+(30-2x)^{2} & \\ \\ =4 \times (30-10) \times 5+(30-10)^{2} & (\text{Put}x=5) \\ \\ =400+400=800 & \end{aligned}$

questions.question_html: Let a curve $y=f(x),x \in (0,\infty)$ pass through the points $P(1,\frac{3}{2})$ and $Q(a,\frac{1}{2})$ . If the tangent at any point $R(b,f(b))$ to the given curve cuts the $y$ -axis at the point $S(0,c)$ such that $bc=3$ , then $(PQ)^{2}$ is equal to __________.
questions.explanation_text: Equation of tangent at $R(b,f(b))$ $y-f(b)=f^{'}(b)(x-b)$ which passes through $S(0,c)$ $\begin{aligned} & \therefore c-f(b)=f^{'}(b)(0-b) \\ \\ & bf^{'}(b)-f(b)=-c \\ \\ & \Rightarrow bf^{'}(b)-f(b)=\frac{-3}{b}( \because bc=3) \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{bf^{'}(b)-f(b)}{b^{2}}=\frac{-3}{b^{3}} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow d(\frac{f(b)}{b})=\frac{-3}{b^{3}} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{f(b)}{b}=\frac{3}{2b^{2}}+c \end{aligned}$ which passes through $P(1,\frac{3}{2})$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \frac{3/2}{1}=\frac{3}{2}+c \\ \\ & \Rightarrow c=0 \\ \\ & \therefore f(b)=\frac{3}{2b^{2}} \times b \\ \\ & \Rightarrow f(b)=\frac{3}{2b} \end{aligned}$ $\because$ It passes through $Q(a,\frac{1}{2})$ $\begin{aligned} & \therefore \frac{1}{2}=\frac{3}{2a} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow a=3 \\ \\ & \therefore P \equiv (1,\frac{3}{2})\text{and}Q \equiv (3,\frac{1}{2}) \\ \\ & \therefore (PQ)^{2}=(3-1)^{2}+(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{3}{2})^{2}=4+1=5 \end{aligned}$

questions.explanation_text: Given, $(xlog_{e}x)f^{'}(x)+(log_{e}x)f(x)+f(x) \ge 1,x \in [2,4]$ $(xlog_{e}x)f^{'}(x)+f(x)[log_{e}x+1] \ge 1$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{d}{dx}[xlog_{e}xf(x)] \ge 1$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \frac{d}{dx}[xlog_{e}xf(x)-x] \ge 0[ \because \frac{d}{dx}(x)=1] \\ \\ & ∀x \in [2,4] \end{aligned}$ Let $g(x)=xlog_{e}xf(x)-x$ As $g(x) \ge 0,∀x \in [2,4],g(x)$ is an increasing function in $[2,4]$ $\begin{aligned} g(2) & =2log_{e}2f(2)-2 \\ \\ & =log_{e}2-2[ \because f(x)=\frac{1}{2}] \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & g(4)=4log_{e}4f(4)-4=log_{e}4-4 \\ \\ & =2(log_{e}2-2) \\ \\ & [ \therefore f(4)=\frac{1}{4}] \end{aligned}$ As, $g(x)$ is an increasing function, $\begin{aligned} & g(2) \le g(x) \le g(4) \\ \\ & log_{e}2-2 \le g(x) \le 2(log_{e}2-2) \\ \\ & log_{e}2-2 \le xlog_{e}xf(x)-x \le 2(log_{e}2-2) \end{aligned}$ $\frac{log_{e}2-2+x}{xlog_{e}x} \le f(x) \le \frac{2(log_{e}2-2)+x}{xlog_{e}x}$ $\begin{aligned} & \text{Now for}x \in [2,4] \\ \\ & \begin{aligned} \frac{log_{e}2-2+x}{xlog_{e}x} & \le \frac{2(log_{e}2-2)+e^{2}}{2log_{e}2}=1-\frac{1}{log_{e}2}<1 \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$ $\Rightarrow f(x) \le 1\text{for}x \in [2,4]$ $\text{Also for}x \in [2,4]\text{:}$ Now, $\begin{aligned} \frac{2(log_{e}2-2)+2}{2log_{e}2} & \ge \frac{log_{e}2-2+4}{4log_{e}4}=\frac{1}{8}+\frac{1}{2log_{e}2}>\frac{1}{8} \end{aligned}$ $\therefore f(x) \ge \frac{1}{8},∀x \in [2,4]$ Hence, both statements $A$ and $B$ are true. Note : LMVT on $(yx(lnx))$ not satisfied. Hence no such function exists. Therefore it should be bonus.
questions.explanation_html:
Given, $(xlog_{e}x)f^{'}(x)+(log_{e}x)f(x)+f(x) \ge 1,x \in [2,4]$

$(xlog_{e}x)f^{'}(x)+f(x)[log_{e}x+1] \ge 1$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{d}{dx}[xlog_{e}xf(x)] \ge 1$

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \frac{d}{dx}[xlog_{e}xf(x)-x] \ge 0[ \because \frac{d}{dx}(x)=1] \\ \\ & ∀x \in [2,4] \end{aligned}$

Let $g(x)=xlog_{e}xf(x)-x$

As $g(x) \ge 0,∀x \in [2,4],g(x)$ is an increasing function in $[2,4]$

$\begin{aligned} g(2) & =2log_{e}2f(2)-2 \\ \\ & =log_{e}2-2[ \because f(x)=\frac{1}{2}] \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & g(4)=4log_{e}4f(4)-4=log_{e}4-4 \\ \\ & =2(log_{e}2-2) \\ \\ & [ \therefore f(4)=\frac{1}{4}] \end{aligned}$

As, $g(x)$ is an increasing function,

$\begin{aligned} & g(2) \le g(x) \le g(4) \\ \\ & log_{e}2-2 \le g(x) \le 2(log_{e}2-2) \\ \\ & log_{e}2-2 \le xlog_{e}xf(x)-x \le 2(log_{e}2-2) \end{aligned}$

$\frac{log_{e}2-2+x}{xlog_{e}x} \le f(x) \le \frac{2(log_{e}2-2)+x}{xlog_{e}x}$

$\begin{aligned} & \text{Now for}x \in [2,4] \\ \\ & \begin{aligned} \frac{log_{e}2-2+x}{xlog_{e}x} & \le \frac{2(log_{e}2-2)+e^{2}}{2log_{e}2}=1-\frac{1}{log_{e}2}<1 \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$

$\Rightarrow f(x) \le 1\text{for}x \in [2,4]$

$\text{Also for}x \in [2,4]\text{:}$

Now,

$\begin{aligned} \frac{2(log_{e}2-2)+2}{2log_{e}2} & \ge \frac{log_{e}2-2+4}{4log_{e}4}=\frac{1}{8}+\frac{1}{2log_{e}2}>\frac{1}{8} \end{aligned}$

$\therefore f(x) \ge \frac{1}{8},∀x \in [2,4]$

Hence, both statements $A$ and $B$ are true.

Note : LMVT on $(yx(lnx))$ not satisfied.

Hence no such function exists.

Therefore it should be bonus.

questions.question_html: The sum of the absolute maximum and minimum values of the function $f(x)=|x^{2}-5x+6|-3x+2$ in the interval $[-1,3]$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: The sum of the absolute maximum and minimum values of the function $f(x)=|x^{2}-5x+6|-3x+2$ in the interval $[-1,3]$ can be found by finding the maximum and minimum values of $f(x)$ in this interval and then adding them. First, let's find the critical points of $f(x)$ . To do this, we will find the zeros of the expression inside the absolute value: $x^{2}-5x+6=0$ Solving this quadratic equation, we find that the zeros are $x=2$ and $x=3$ . These are the critical points of $f(x)$ . So, the sum of the absolute maximum and minimum values of the function is $-7+17=10$ . questions.question_html:
Consider the triangles with vertices $A(2,1),B(0,0)$ and $C(t,4),t \in [0,4]$ .

If the maximum and the minimum perimeters of such triangles are obtained at

$t=\alpha$ and $t=\beta$ respectively, then $6\alpha+21\beta$ is equal to ___________.
questions.explanation_text: We have a triangle with vertices $A(2,1)$ , $B(0,0)$ , and $C(t,4)$ , where $t$ belongs to the interval $[0,4]$ . We want to find the maximum and minimum perimeters of such triangles, which occur at $t=\alpha$ and $t=\beta$ , respectively. To find the minimum perimeter, we use a geometric approach. Reflect point $B$ over the line $y=4$ to get $B^{'}(0,8)$ . The line segment $AB^{'}$ intersects the line $y=4$ (which is the $y$ -coordinate of point $C$ ) at the point which gives the minimum perimeter. The slope of $AB^{'}$ is : $m_{AB^{'}}=\frac{8-1}{0-2}=\frac{-7}{2}$ The equation of the line $AB^{'}$ is then $y-1=m_{AB^{'}}(x-2)$ , or $7x+2y=16$ . Solving this equation for $y=4$ yields $x=\frac{8}{7}$ . So, the minimum perimeter is achieved at point $C(\frac{8}{7},4)$ , so $\beta=\frac{8}{7}$ . For the maximum perimeter, we notice that it will be achieved when point $C$ is either at $(0,4)$ or at $(4,4)$ , since these are the furthest points from $A(2,1)$ within the range of $t$ . By calculating the perimeters at these points, we find that the maximum perimeter is achieved at $\alpha=4$ . Finally, we calculate $6\alpha+21\beta=6 \cdot 4+21 \cdot \frac{8}{7}=24+24=48$ . Therefore, $6\alpha+21\beta=48$ .

The slope of $AB^{'}$ is :

$m_{AB^{'}}=\frac{8-1}{0-2}=\frac{-7}{2}$

The equation of the line $AB^{'}$ is then $y-1=m_{AB^{'}}(x-2)$ , or $7x+2y=16$ .

Solving this equation for $y=4$ yields $x=\frac{8}{7}$ . So, the minimum perimeter is achieved at point $C(\frac{8}{7},4)$ , so $\beta=\frac{8}{7}$ .

For the maximum perimeter, we notice that it will be achieved when point $C$ is either at $(0,4)$ or at $(4,4)$ , since these are the furthest points from $A(2,1)$ within the range of $t$ . Therefore, $6\alpha+21\beta=48$ .

questions.question_html: The number of points, where the curve $y=x^{5}-20x^{3}+50x+2$ crosses the $x$ -axis, is ____________.
questions.explanation_text: Given equation of curve $\begin{aligned} & y=x^{5}-20x^{3}+50x+2 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}=5x^{4}-60x^{2}+50 \end{aligned}$ On putting $\frac{dy}{dx}=0$ $\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow & 5(x^{4}-12x^{2}+10)=0 \\ \\ \Rightarrow & x^{2}=\frac{12 \pm \sqrt{144-40}}{2}=6 \pm \sqrt{26} \\ \\ \Rightarrow & x^{2}=6-\sqrt{26},6+\sqrt{26} \\ \\ \Rightarrow & x^{2}=6-5.10,6+5.10 \\ \\ \Rightarrow & x^{2}=09,11.1 \\ \\ \Rightarrow & x= \pm \sqrt{0.9}, \pm \sqrt{11.1} \\ \\ \Rightarrow & x=-0.95,0.95,-3.33,3.33 \end{aligned}$ Now, $\begin{aligned} y(0) & =2(+ve) \Rightarrow y(1)=+ve \\ \\ y(2) & =-ve \Rightarrow y(3.3)=-ve \\ \\ y(-1) & =-ve \Rightarrow y(-2)=+ve \\ \\ y(-3.3) & =-ve \end{aligned}$ $\because \text{Required number of points}=5$

questions.explanation_text: Let the quadratic curve be $f(x)=ax^{2}+bx+c$ The curve passes through $(-1,0)$ $0=a-b+c \Rightarrow a+c=b$ ..........(i) The curve also passes through $(1,1)$ $\begin{aligned} a+b+c=1.........(ii) \\ \\ 2b=1 \Rightarrow b=\frac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$ $f^{'}(x)=2ax+b$ Slope tangent of curve $=f^{'}(x)$ at $(1,1)=2a+b$ Slope of line $y=x$ is 1 $\begin{aligned} & \therefore 2a+b=1 \\ \\ & 2a+\frac{1}{2}=1 \Rightarrow a=\frac{1}{4} \\ \\ & c=1-a-b \Rightarrow c=\frac{1}{4} \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & f(x)=\frac{1}{4}x^{2}+\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{4}=\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{4} \\ \\ & f^{'}(x)=\frac{2(x+1)}{4}=\frac{x+1}{2} \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & f(x)\text{passes through}(\alpha,\alpha+1) \\ \\ & \begin{aligned} \therefore \alpha+1=\frac{(\alpha+1)^{2}}{4} \\ \\ \Rightarrow \alpha+1=4\text{or}\alpha=3 \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$ Equation of normal at $(3,4)$ is $y-4=-\frac{1}{2}(x-3)$ For $x$ , intercept, $y=0$ $x-3=8\text{or}x=11$ Hence, the required $x$ intercept is 11 .

$\begin{aligned} & f(x)\text{passes through}(\alpha,\alpha+1) \\ \\ & \begin{aligned} \therefore \alpha+1=\frac{(\alpha+1)^{2}}{4} \\ \\ \Rightarrow \alpha+1=4\text{or}\alpha=3 \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$

$y-4=-\frac{1}{2}(x-3)$

questions.explanation_text: Given curve : $y=\frac{x-a}{(x+b)(x-2)}$ at $(1,-3)$ $\therefore$ $-3=\frac{1-a}{(1+b)(-1)} \Rightarrow 3+3b=1-a$ $\beta \Rightarrow a+3b+2=0$ $y=\frac{x-a}{(x+b)(x-2)}$ $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{(x+b)(x-2)-(x-a)[(x+b)+(x-2)]}{[(x+b)(x-2)]^{2}}$ at $(1,-3)m_{T}=\frac{-(1+b)-(1-a)(b)}{(1+b)^{2}}=-4$ $\therefore$ $1+b+b-ab=4(1+b)^{2}$ $\Rightarrow 1+2b+b(3b+2)=4b^{2}+4+8b$ $\Rightarrow b^{2}+4b+3=0$ $(b+1)(b+3)=0$ $b=-1,a=1$ but $1+b \ne 0$ $b=-3,a=7$ $\therefore$ $b \ne -1$ $\therefore$ $a+b=04$
questions.explanation_html:
Given curve : $y=\frac{x-a}{(x+b)(x-2)}$ at $(1,-3)$

$\therefore$ $-3=\frac{1-a}{(1+b)(-1)} \Rightarrow 3+3b=1-a$

$\beta \Rightarrow a+3b+2=0$

$y=\frac{x-a}{(x+b)(x-2)}$

$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{(x+b)(x-2)-(x-a)[(x+b)+(x-2)]}{[(x+b)(x-2)]^{2}}$

at $(1,-3)m_{T}=\frac{-(1+b)-(1-a)(b)}{(1+b)^{2}}=-4$

questions.explanation_text: $\text{Given,}$ $\begin{aligned} f_{a}(x) & =tan^{-1}2x-3ax+7 \\ \\ f_{a}^{'}(x) & =\frac{2}{1+4x^{2}}-3a \end{aligned}$ As the function $f_{a}^{'}(x)$ is non-decreasing $\begin{aligned} & \text{in}(-\frac{\pi}{6},\frac{\pi}{6}), \\ \\ & f_{a}^{'}(x) \ge 0 \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \frac{2}{1+4x^{2}}-3a \ge 0 \Rightarrow \frac{2}{1+4x^{2}} \ge 3a \\ \\ & \Rightarrow a \le \frac{2}{3(1+4x^{2})},\text{when}x \in (-\frac{\pi}{6},\frac{\pi}{6}) \\ \\ & \because a\text{is maximum when}x^{2}=\frac{\pi^{2}}{36}, \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} a_{max} & =\frac{2}{3(1+\frac{4\pi^{2}}{36})}=\frac{2 \times 12}{36+4\pi^{2}} \\ \\ & =\frac{6}{9+\pi^{2}} \\ \\ \therefore \bar{a} & =\frac{6}{9+\pi^{2}} \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & \therefore f_{a}(x)=tan^{-1}2x-\frac{18}{9+\pi^{2}}x+7 \\ \\ & f_{\pi}(\frac{\pi}{8})=tan^{-1}2(\frac{\pi}{8})-\frac{18}{9+\pi^{2}} \times \frac{\pi}{8}+7 \\ \\ & =tan^{-1}\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac{9\pi}{36+4\pi^{2}}+7 \\ \\ & =8-\frac{9\pi}{36+4\pi^{2}}=8-\frac{9\pi}{4(9+\pi^{2})} \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
$\text{Given,}$

$\begin{aligned} f_{a}(x) & =tan^{-1}2x-3ax+7 \\ \\ f_{a}^{'}(x) & =\frac{2}{1+4x^{2}}-3a \end{aligned}$

As the function $f_{a}^{'}(x)$ is non-decreasing

$\begin{aligned} & \text{in}(-\frac{\pi}{6},\frac{\pi}{6}), \\ \\ & f_{a}^{'}(x) \ge 0 \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \frac{2}{1+4x^{2}}-3a \ge 0 \Rightarrow \frac{2}{1+4x^{2}} \ge 3a \\ \\ & \Rightarrow a \le \frac{2}{3(1+4x^{2})},\text{when}x \in (-\frac{\pi}{6},\frac{\pi}{6}) \\ \\ & \because a\text{is maximum when}x^{2}=\frac{\pi^{2}}{36}, \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} a_{max} & =\frac{2}{3(1+\frac{4\pi^{2}}{36})}=\frac{2 \times 12}{36+4\pi^{2}} \\ \\ & =\frac{6}{9+\pi^{2}} \\ \\ \therefore \bar{a} & =\frac{6}{9+\pi^{2}} \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & \therefore f_{a}(x)=tan^{-1}2x-\frac{18}{9+\pi^{2}}x+7 \\ \\ & f_{\pi}(\frac{\pi}{8})=tan^{-1}2(\frac{\pi}{8})-\frac{18}{9+\pi^{2}} \times \frac{\pi}{8}+7 \\ \\ & =tan^{-1}\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac{9\pi}{36+4\pi^{2}}+7 \\ \\ & =8-\frac{9\pi}{36+4\pi^{2}}=8-\frac{9\pi}{4(9+\pi^{2})} \end{aligned}$

Also, $f^{'}(x)$ is negative before $\frac{4}{3}$ means slope of f(x) is negative before $\frac{4}{3}$ and f'(x) is positive after $\frac{4}{3}$ means slope of f(x) is positive after $\frac{4}{3}$ .

$\therefore$ At $\frac{4}{3},f(x)$ is local minimum

From wavy curve method,

$f^{'}(x)>0,∀x \in (-\alpha,\frac{1}{2})∪(\frac{4}{3},\alpha)$

$\therefore$ f(x) increasing in $x \in (-\alpha,\frac{1}{2})∪(\frac{4}{3},\alpha)$

$f^{'}(x)<0∀x \in (\frac{1}{2},\frac{4}{3})$

$\therefore$ f(x) decreasing in $x \in (\frac{1}{2},\frac{4}{3})$

questions.question_html: The surface area of a balloon of spherical shape being inflated, increases at a constant rate. If initially, the radius of balloon is 3 units and after 5 seconds, it becomes 7 units, then its radius after 9 seconds is :
questions.explanation_text: We know, Surface area of balloon (s) = 4 $\pi$ r 2 $\therefore$ $\frac{ds}{dt}=\frac{d}{dt}(4\pi r^{2})$ $\Rightarrow \frac{ds}{dt}=4\pi(2r) \times \frac{dr}{dt}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{ds}{dt}=8\pi r \times \frac{dr}{dt}$ Given that, surface area of balloon is increasing in constant rate. $\therefore$ $\frac{ds}{dt}$ = constant = k (Assume) $\Rightarrow k=8\pi r.\frac{dr}{dt}$ $\Rightarrow \int kdt=\int 8\pi rdr$ $\Rightarrow kt=8\pi \times \frac{r^{2}}{2}+c$ $\Rightarrow kt=4\pi r^{2}+c$ ..... (1) Given at t = 0, radius r = 3 So, $0=4\pi(3^{2})+c$ $\Rightarrow c=-36\pi$ $\therefore$ Equation (1) becomes $kt=4\pi r^{2}-36\pi$ Also given, at t = 5, radius r = 7 $\therefore$ $k(5)=4\pi(7)^{2}-36$ $\Rightarrow k=32\pi$ $\therefore$ Equation (1) is $32\pi t=4\pi r^{2}-36\pi$ Now at $t=9$ $\Rightarrow 32\pi(9)=4\pi r^{2}-36\pi$ $\Rightarrow 8 \times 9=r^{2}-9$ $\Rightarrow r^{2}=81 \Rightarrow r=9$

questions.question_text: If the tangent to the curve $y=x^{3}-x^{2}+x$ at the point $(a,b)$ is also tangent to the curve $y=5x^{2}+2x-25$ at the point (2, $-$ 1), then $|2a+9b|$ is equal to __________.
questions.question_html: If the tangent to the curve $y=x^{3}-x^{2}+x$ at the point $(a,b)$ is also tangent to the curve $y=5x^{2}+2x-25$ at the point (2, $-$ 1), then $|2a+9b|$ is equal to __________.
questions.explanation_text: Slope of tangent to curve $y=5x^{2}+2x-25$ $=m=(\frac{dy}{dx})_{at(2,-1)}=22$ $\therefore$ Equation of tangent $:y+1=22(x-2)$ $\therefore y=22x-45$ . Slope of tangent to $y=x^{3}-x^{2}+x$ at point $(a,b)$ $=3a^{2}-2a+1$ $3a^{2}-2a+1=22$ $3a^{2}-2a-21=0$ $\therefore a=3$ or $-\frac{7}{3}$ Also $b=a^{3}-a^{2}+a$ Then $(a,b)=(3,21)$ or $(-\frac{7}{3},-\frac{151}{9})$ . $(-\frac{7}{3},-\frac{151}{9})$ does not satisfy the equation of tangent $\therefore a=3,b=21$ $\therefore |2a+9b|=195$
questions.explanation_html:
Slope of tangent to curve $y=5x^{2}+2x-25$

$=m=(\frac{dy}{dx})_{at(2,-1)}=22$

$\therefore$ Equation of tangent $:y+1=22(x-2)$

$\therefore y=22x-45$ .

Slope of tangent to $y=x^{3}-x^{2}+x$ at point $(a,b)$

$=3a^{2}-2a+1$

$3a^{2}-2a+1=22$

$3a^{2}-2a-21=0$

$\therefore a=3$ or $-\frac{7}{3}$

Also $b=a^{3}-a^{2}+a$

Then $(a,b)=(3,21)$ or $(-\frac{7}{3},-\frac{151}{9})$ .

$(-\frac{7}{3},-\frac{151}{9})$ does not satisfy the equation of tangent

$\therefore a=3,b=21$

$\therefore |2a+9b|=195$

questions.question_html: The sum of the maximum and minimum values of the function $f(x)=|5x-7|+[x^{2}+2x]$ in the interval $[\frac{5}{4},2]$ , where $[t]$ is the greatest integer $\le t$ , is ______________.
questions.explanation_text: $f(x)=|5x-7|+[x^{2}+2x]$ $=|5x-7|+[(x+1)^{2}]-1$ Critical points of $f(x)=\frac{7}{5},\sqrt{5}-1,\sqrt{6}-1,\sqrt{7}-1,\sqrt{8}-1,2$ $\therefore$ Maximum or minimum value of $f(x)$ occur at critical points or boundary points $\therefore$ $f(\frac{5}{4})=\frac{3}{4}+4=\frac{19}{4}$ $f(\frac{7}{5})=0+4=4$ as both $|5x-7|$ and $x^{2}+2x$ are increasing in nature after $x=\frac{7}{5}$ $\therefore$ $f(2)=3+8=11$ $\therefore$ $f(\frac{7}{5})_{min}=4$ and $f(2)_{max}=11$ Sum is $4+11=15$

$=|5x-7|+[(x+1)^{2}]-1$

Critical points of

$f(x)=\frac{7}{5},\sqrt{5}-1,\sqrt{6}-1,\sqrt{7}-1,\sqrt{8}-1,2$

$\therefore$ Maximum or minimum value of $f(x)$ occur at critical points or boundary points

as both $|5x-7|$ and $x^{2}+2x$ are increasing in nature after $x=\frac{7}{5}$

$\therefore$ $f(\frac{7}{5})_{min}=4$ and $f(2)_{max}=11$

Sum is $4+11=15$

questions.explanation_text: Given, $f(x)=(-3)^{n_{1}}(x-5)^{n_{2}}$ Differentiating both side with respect to x, we get $f^{'}(x)=(x-5)^{n_{2}}(n_{1}(x-3)^{n_{1}-1})+(x-3)^{n_{1}}(n_{2}(x-5)^{n_{2}-1})$ $=(x-3)^{n_{1}}(x-5)^{n_{2}}[\frac{n_{1}}{x-3}+\frac{n_{2}}{x-5}]$ $=(x-3)^{n_{1}}(x-5)^{n_{2}}[\frac{n_{1}(x-5)+n_{2}(x-3)}{(x-3)(x-5)}]$ $=(x-3)^{n_{1}-1}(x-5)^{n_{2}-1}[n_{1}(x-5)+n_{2}(x-3)]$ Option A : When n 1 = 3 and n 2 = 4 then $f^{'}(x)=(x-3)^{3-1}(x-5)^{4-1}[3(x-5)+4(x-3)]$ $=(x-3)^{2}(x-5)^{3}(7x-27)$ Critical point is at x = 3, 5 and $\frac{27}{7}$ When value of f'(x) is less than $\frac{27}{5}$ , f'(x) is positive means slope of f(x) graph is positive. And when f'(x) is greater than $\frac{29}{7}$ but less than 5 then f'(x) is positive means slope of graph of f(x) is positive. So at $\frac{29}{7}$ between 3 and 5, f(x) attain local minima. $\therefore$ Option (B) is correct. Option C : When n 1 = 3 and n 2 = 5 then $f^{'}(x)=(x-3)^{3-1}(x-5)^{5-1}[3(x-5)+5(x-3)]$ $=(x-3)^{2}(x-5)^{4}(8x-30)$ Critical point is at x = 3, 5 and $\frac{30}{8}$ When f'(x) is less than $\frac{30}{8}$ but greater than 3 then f'(x) is negative means slope of graph of f(x) is negative. And when f'(x) is greater than $\frac{30}{8}$ but less than 5 then f'(x) is positive means slope of graph of f(x) is positive. So, at $\frac{30}{8}$ between 3 and 5, f(x) attain local minima. $\therefore$ Option C is not true. Similarly you can check option D also.

Assume that the rate at which the virus spreads is directly proportional to the product of the number of infected students and the number of non-infected students. If the number of infected students on 4 th day is 30, then number of infected students on 8 th day will be __________.
questions.question_html: A hostel has 100 students. On a certain day (consider it day zero) it was found that two students are infected with some virus. Assume that the rate at which the virus spreads is directly proportional to the product of the number of infected students and the number of non-infected students. If the number of infected students on 4th day is 30, then number of infected students on 8th day will be __________.
questions.explanation_text: Total students = 100 At t = 0 (zero day), infected student = 2 Let at t = t day infected student = x $\therefore$ At t = t day non infected student = (100 $-$ x) Rate of infection $=\frac{dx}{dt}$ Given, $\frac{dx}{dt}∝x(100-x)$ $\Rightarrow \int\frac{dx}{x(100-x)}=\intkdt$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{100}\int\frac{100-x+x}{x(100-x)}dx=kt+c$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{100}\int(\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{100-x})dx=kt+c$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{100}[lnx-ln(100-x)]=kt+c$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{100}ln\frac{x}{100-x}=kt+c$ ...... (1) Given, At, t = 0, x = 2 $\therefore$ $\frac{1}{100}ln\frac{2}{98}=c$ Putting value of c in equation (1), we get $\frac{1}{100}ln\frac{x}{100-x}=kt+\frac{1}{100}ln\frac{2}{98}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{100}ln\frac{x}{100-x}-\frac{1}{100}ln\frac{2}{98}=kt$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{100}ln\frac{x \times 98}{2(100-x)}=kt$ Given, At t = 4, x = 30 $\therefore$ $\frac{1}{100}ln\frac{30 \times 98}{2(70)}=k \times 4$ $\Rightarrow k=\frac{1}{400}ln21$ $\therefore$ $\frac{1}{100}ln\frac{x \times 98}{2(100-x)}=t \times \frac{1}{400} \times ln21$ Now, when t = 8, then r = ? $\frac{1}{100}ln\frac{49x}{(100-x)}=8 \times \frac{1}{400} \times ln21$ $\Rightarrow ln\frac{49x}{(100-x)}=2ln21$ $\Rightarrow \frac{49x}{100-x}=21^{2}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{x}{100-x}=\frac{21 \times 21}{49}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{x}{100-x}=9$ $\Rightarrow x=900-9x$ $\Rightarrow 10x=900$ $\Rightarrow x=90$
questions.explanation_html:
Total students = 100

At t = 0 (zero day), infected student = 2

Let at t = t day infected student = x

$\therefore$ At t = t day non infected student = (100 $-$ x)

Rate of infection $=\frac{dx}{dt}$

Given, $\frac{dx}{dt}∝x(100-x)$

$\Rightarrow \int\frac{dx}{x(100-x)}=\intkdt$

$\Rightarrow \frac{1}{100}\int\frac{100-x+x}{x(100-x)}dx=kt+c$

$\Rightarrow \frac{1}{100}\int(\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{100-x})dx=kt+c$

$\Rightarrow \frac{1}{100}[lnx-ln(100-x)]=kt+c$

$\Rightarrow \frac{1}{100}ln\frac{x}{100-x}=kt+c$ ...... (1)

Given, At, t = 0, x = 2

$\therefore$ $\frac{1}{100}ln\frac{2}{98}=c$

Putting value of c in equation (1), we get

$\frac{1}{100}ln\frac{x}{100-x}=kt+\frac{1}{100}ln\frac{2}{98}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{1}{100}ln\frac{x}{100-x}-\frac{1}{100}ln\frac{2}{98}=kt$

$\Rightarrow \frac{1}{100}ln\frac{x \times 98}{2(100-x)}=kt$

Given, At t = 4, x = 30

$\therefore$ $\frac{1}{100}ln\frac{30 \times 98}{2(70)}=k \times 4$

$\Rightarrow k=\frac{1}{400}ln21$

$\therefore$ $\frac{1}{100}ln\frac{x \times 98}{2(100-x)}=t \times \frac{1}{400} \times ln21$

Now, when t = 8, then r = ?

$\frac{1}{100}ln\frac{49x}{(100-x)}=8 \times \frac{1}{400} \times ln21$

$\Rightarrow ln\frac{49x}{(100-x)}=2ln21$

$\Rightarrow \frac{49x}{100-x}=21^{2}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{x}{100-x}=\frac{21 \times 21}{49}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{x}{100-x}=9$

$\Rightarrow x=900-9x$

$\Rightarrow 10x=900$

$\Rightarrow x=90$

questions.question_html: The curve $y(x)=ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx+5$ touches the $x$ -axis at the point $P(-2,0)$ and cuts the $y$ -axis at the point $Q$ , where $y^{'}$ is equal to 3 . Then the local maximum value of $y(x)$ is:
questions.explanation_text: $f(x)=y=ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx+5\dots$ (i) $\frac{dy}{dx}=3ax^{2}+2bx+c\dots(ii)$ Touches $x$ -axis at $P(-2,0)$ $\Rightarrow y|_{x=-2}=0 \Rightarrow -8a+4b-2c+5=0\dots...(iii)$ Touches $x$ -axis at $P(-2,0)$ also implies $\frac{dy}{dx}|_{x=-2}=0 \Rightarrow 12a-4b+c=0\dots...(iv)$ $y=f(x)$ cuts $y$ -axis at $(0,5)$ Given, $\frac{dy}{dx}|_{x=0}=c=3$ From (iii), (iv) and (v) $\begin{aligned} & a=-\frac{1}{2},b=-\frac{3}{4},c=3 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow f(x)=\frac{-x^{2}}{2}-\frac{3}{4}x^{2}+3x+5 \\ \\ & f^{'}(x)=\frac{-3}{2}x^{2}-\frac{3}{2}x+3 \\ \\ & =\frac{-3}{2}(x+2)(x-1) \\ \\ & f^{'}(x)=0\text{at}x=-2\text{and}x=1 \end{aligned}$ By first derivative test $x=1$ in point of local maximum Hence local maximum value of $f(x)$ is $f(1)$ i.e., $\frac{27}{4}$

$\Rightarrow y|_{x=-2}=0 \Rightarrow -8a+4b-2c+5=0\dots...(iii)$

Touches $x$ -axis at $P(-2,0)$ also implies

$\frac{dy}{dx}|_{x=-2}=0 \Rightarrow 12a-4b+c=0\dots...(iv)$

$y=f(x)$ cuts $y$ -axis at $(0,5)$

Given, $\frac{dy}{dx}|_{x=0}=c=3$

From (iii), (iv) and (v)

$\begin{aligned} & a=-\frac{1}{2},b=-\frac{3}{4},c=3 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow f(x)=\frac{-x^{2}}{2}-\frac{3}{4}x^{2}+3x+5 \\ \\ & f^{'}(x)=\frac{-3}{2}x^{2}-\frac{3}{2}x+3 \\ \\ & =\frac{-3}{2}(x+2)(x-1) \\ \\ & f^{'}(x)=0\text{at}x=-2\text{and}x=1 \end{aligned}$

By first derivative test $x=1$ in point of local maximum Hence local maximum value of $f(x)$ is $f(1)$

i.e., $\frac{27}{4}$

questions.question_text: Let S be the set of all the natural numbers, for which the line $\frac{x}{a}+\frac{y}{b}=2$ is a tangent to the curve $(\frac{x}{a})^{n}+(\frac{y}{b})^{n}=2$ at the point (a, b), ab $\ne$ 0. Then :
questions.question_html: Let S be the set of all the natural numbers, for which the line $\frac{x}{a}+\frac{y}{b}=2$ is a tangent to the curve $(\frac{x}{a})^{n}+(\frac{y}{b})^{n}=2$ at the point (a, b), ab $\ne$ 0. Then :

options.label: C
options.html: S = {2k : k $\in$ N}

questions.explanation_text: $(\frac{x}{a})^{n}+(\frac{y}{b})^{n}=2$ Differentiating both sides with respect to x, we get $\Rightarrow n.(\frac{x}{a})^{n-a}.\frac{1}{a}+n.(\frac{y}{b})^{n-1}.\frac{1}{b}.\frac{dy}{dx}=0$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{\frac{1}{a}.(\frac{x}{a})^{n-1}}{\frac{1}{b}(\frac{y}{b})^{n-1}}$ $=-\frac{b}{a}(\frac{xb}{ya})^{n-1}$ Now, $\frac{dy}{dx}$ at (a, b) $=-\frac{b}{a}[\frac{ab}{ba}]^{n-1}=-\frac{b}{a}$ Equation of tangent at (a, b) is, $(y-b)=-\frac{b}{a}(x-a)$ $\Rightarrow \frac{y-b}{b}=-\frac{x-a}{a}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{y}{b}-1=-\frac{x}{a}+1$ $\Rightarrow \frac{x}{a}+\frac{y}{b}=2$ $\therefore$ It is tangent for all value of n.
questions.explanation_html:
$(\frac{x}{a})^{n}+(\frac{y}{b})^{n}=2$

Differentiating both sides with respect to x, we get

$\Rightarrow n.(\frac{x}{a})^{n-a}.\frac{1}{a}+n.(\frac{y}{b})^{n-1}.\frac{1}{b}.\frac{dy}{dx}=0$

$\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{\frac{1}{a}.(\frac{x}{a})^{n-1}}{\frac{1}{b}(\frac{y}{b})^{n-1}}$

$=-\frac{b}{a}(\frac{xb}{ya})^{n-1}$

Now, $\frac{dy}{dx}$ at (a, b) $=-\frac{b}{a}[\frac{ab}{ba}]^{n-1}=-\frac{b}{a}$

Equation of tangent at (a, b) is,

$(y-b)=-\frac{b}{a}(x-a)$

$\Rightarrow \frac{y-b}{b}=-\frac{x-a}{a}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{y}{b}-1=-\frac{x}{a}+1$

$\Rightarrow \frac{x}{a}+\frac{y}{b}=2$

$\therefore$ It is tangent for all value of n.

questions.question_html: If xy4 attains maximum value at the point (x, y) on the line passing through the points (50 + $\alpha$ , 0) and (0, 50 + $\alpha$ ), $\alpha$ > 0, then (x, y) also lies on the line :
questions.explanation_text: Equation of line passing through the point (50 + $\alpha$ , 0) and (0, 50 + $\alpha$ ) is $y-0=\frac{50+\alpha-0}{0-(50+\alpha)}(x-(50+\alpha))$ $\Rightarrow y=-1(x-(50+\alpha))$ $\Rightarrow y=(50+\alpha)-x$ $\Rightarrow x+y=50+\alpha$ Let $p=xy^{4}$ $=(50+\alpha-y)y^{4}$ $=(50+\alpha)y^{4}-y^{5}$ For maximum or minimum value of p, $\frac{dp}{dy}=0$ $\Rightarrow 4y^{3}(50+\alpha)-5y^{4}=0$ $\Rightarrow y^{3}[200+4\alpha-5y]=0$ $\therefore$ $y=0$ or $200+4\alpha-5y=0$ $\Rightarrow y=\frac{4}{5}(50+\alpha)$ $\therefore$ $x=50+\alpha-y$ $=50+\alpha-\frac{4}{5}(50+\alpha)$ $=50+\alpha(1-\frac{4}{5})$ $=\frac{1}{5}(50+\alpha)$ $\Rightarrow 4x=\frac{4}{5}(50+\alpha)=y$ $\Rightarrow y=4x$ $\therefore$ (x, y) lies on the line y = 4x
questions.explanation_html:
Equation of line passing through the point (50 + $\alpha$ , 0) and (0, 50 + $\alpha$ ) is

$y-0=\frac{50+\alpha-0}{0-(50+\alpha)}(x-(50+\alpha))$

$\Rightarrow y=-1(x-(50+\alpha))$

$\Rightarrow y=(50+\alpha)-x$

$\Rightarrow x+y=50+\alpha$

Let $p=xy^{4}$

$=(50+\alpha-y)y^{4}$

$=(50+\alpha)y^{4}-y^{5}$

For maximum or minimum value of p,

$\frac{dp}{dy}=0$

$\Rightarrow 4y^{3}(50+\alpha)-5y^{4}=0$

$\Rightarrow y^{3}[200+4\alpha-5y]=0$

$\therefore$ $y=0$

or

$200+4\alpha-5y=0$

$\Rightarrow y=\frac{4}{5}(50+\alpha)$

$\therefore$ $x=50+\alpha-y$

$=50+\alpha-\frac{4}{5}(50+\alpha)$

$=50+\alpha(1-\frac{4}{5})$

$=\frac{1}{5}(50+\alpha)$

$\Rightarrow 4x=\frac{4}{5}(50+\alpha)=y$

$\Rightarrow y=4x$

$\therefore$ (x, y) lies on the line y = 4x

questions.question_html: The sum of absolute maximum and absolute minimum values of the function $f(x)=|2x^{2}+3x-2|+sinxcosx$ in the interval [0, 1] is :
questions.explanation_text: $f(x)=|(2x-1)(x+2)|+\frac{sin2x}{2}$ $0 \le x<\frac{1}{2}f(x)=(1-2x)(x+2)+\frac{sin2x}{2}$ $f^{'}(x)=-4x-3+cos2x<0$ For $x \ge \frac{1}{2}:f^{'}(x)=4x+3+cos2x>0$ So, minima occurs at $x=\frac{1}{2}$ $\begin{aligned} f(x)|_{min} & =|2(\frac{1}{2})^{2}+\frac{3}{2}-2|+sin(\frac{1}{2}) \cdot cos(\frac{1}{2}) \\ \\ & =\frac{1}{2}sin1 \end{aligned}$ So, maxima is possible at $x=0$ or $x=1$ Now checking for $x=0$ and $x=1$ , we can see it attains its maximum value at $x=1$ $\begin{aligned} f(x)|_{max}= & |2+3-2|+\frac{sin2}{2} \\ \\ & =3+\frac{1}{2}sin2 \end{aligned}$ Sum of absolute maximum and minimum value $=3+\frac{1}{2}(sin1+sin2)$ $=3+\frac{1}{2}(sin1+2sin1cos1)$ = $3+\frac{1}{2}(1+2cos(1))sin(1)$
questions.explanation_html:
$f(x)=|(2x-1)(x+2)|+\frac{sin2x}{2}$

$0 \le x<\frac{1}{2}f(x)=(1-2x)(x+2)+\frac{sin2x}{2}$

$f^{'}(x)=-4x-3+cos2x<0$

For $x \ge \frac{1}{2}:f^{'}(x)=4x+3+cos2x>0$

So, minima occurs at $x=\frac{1}{2}$

$\begin{aligned} f(x)|_{min} & =|2(\frac{1}{2})^{2}+\frac{3}{2}-2|+sin(\frac{1}{2}) \cdot cos(\frac{1}{2}) \\ \\ & =\frac{1}{2}sin1 \end{aligned}$

So, maxima is possible at $x=0$ or $x=1$

Now checking for $x=0$ and $x=1$ , we can see it attains its maximum value at $x=1$

$\begin{aligned} f(x)|_{max}= & |2+3-2|+\frac{sin2}{2} \\ \\ & =3+\frac{1}{2}sin2 \end{aligned}$

Sum of absolute maximum and minimum value

$=3+\frac{1}{2}(sin1+sin2)$

$=3+\frac{1}{2}(sin1+2sin1cos1)$

= $3+\frac{1}{2}(1+2cos(1))sin(1)$

questions.explanation_text: $\delta^{'}(x)=\frac{4x^{2}-1}{x}$ so f(x) is decreasing in $(0,\frac{1}{2})$ and increasing in $(\frac{1}{2},\infty) \Rightarrow a=\frac{1}{2}$ Tangent at $y^{2}=2x \Rightarrow y=,x+\frac{1}{2m}$ It is passing through $(4,3)$ $3=4m+\frac{1}{2m} \Rightarrow m=\frac{1}{2}$ or $\frac{1}{4}$ So tangent may be $y=\frac{1}{2}x+1$ or $y=\frac{1}{4}x+2$ But $y=\frac{1}{2}x+1$ passes through $(-2,0)$ so rejected. questions.explanation_text: $\frac{x^{2}}{a}+\frac{y^{2}}{b}=1$ ..........(1) Differentiating both sides : $\frac{2x}{a}+\frac{2y}{b}\frac{dy}{dx}=0 \Rightarrow \frac{y}{b}\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-x}{a}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-bx}{ay}$ ............(2) $\frac{x^{2}}{c}+\frac{y^{2}}{d}=1$ ........(3) Differentiating both sides : $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-dx}{cy}$ ...........(4) $m_{1}m_{2}=-1 \Rightarrow \frac{-bx}{ay} \times \frac{-dx}{cy}=-1$ $\Rightarrow bdx^{2}=-acy^{2}$ .............(5) $(1)-(3) \Rightarrow (\frac{1}{a}-\frac{1}{c})x^{2}+(\frac{1}{b}-\frac{1}{d})y^{2}=0$ $\Rightarrow \frac{c-a}{ac}x^{2}+\frac{d-b}{bd} \times (\frac{-bd}{ac})x^{2}=0$ (using 5) $\Rightarrow (c-a)-(d-b)=0$ $\Rightarrow c-a=d-b$ $\Rightarrow c-d=a-b$
questions.explanation_html:
$\frac{x^{2}}{a}+\frac{y^{2}}{b}=1$ ..........(1)

Differentiating both sides :

$\frac{2x}{a}+\frac{2y}{b}\frac{dy}{dx}=0 \Rightarrow \frac{y}{b}\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-x}{a}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-bx}{ay}$ ............(2)

$\frac{x^{2}}{c}+\frac{y^{2}}{d}=1$ ........(3)

Differentiating both sides : $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-dx}{cy}$ ...........(4)

$m_{1}m_{2}=-1 \Rightarrow \frac{-bx}{ay} \times \frac{-dx}{cy}=-1$

$\Rightarrow bdx^{2}=-acy^{2}$ .............(5)

$(1)-(3) \Rightarrow (\frac{1}{a}-\frac{1}{c})x^{2}+(\frac{1}{b}-\frac{1}{d})y^{2}=0$

$\Rightarrow \frac{c-a}{ac}x^{2}+\frac{d-b}{bd} \times (\frac{-bd}{ac})x^{2}=0$ (using 5)

$\Rightarrow (c-a)-(d-b)=0$

$\Rightarrow c-a=d-b$

$\Rightarrow c-d=a-b$

(ii) Also, $-2\sqrt{2}b-4=8-4a+c$ $4a-2\sqrt{2}b-c=12$ .... (iii) Also, $a-2\sqrt{2}b=3$ .... (iv) (given) $(ii)-(iii) \Rightarrow -a+(2\sqrt{2}-3)b=-3$ ... As it passes through (a, b)

$b-y=-\frac{1}{m}(a-x)=-\frac{dx}{dy}(a-x)$

$\Rightarrow (b-y)dy=(x-a)dx$

by $-\frac{y^{2}}{2}=\frac{x^{2}}{2}-ax+c$ ..... (i)

questions.question_text: The function f(x) = $\frac{4x^{3}-3x^{2}}{6}-2sinx+(2x-1)cosx$ :
questions.question_html:
The function
f(x) = $\frac{4x^{3}-3x^{2}}{6}-2sinx+(2x-1)cosx$ :
questions.explanation_text: Given, $f(x)=\frac{4x^{3}-3x^{2}}{6}-2sinx+(2x-1)cosx$ $f^{'}(x)=\frac{12x^{2}-6x}{6}-2cosx+(2x-1)(-sinx)+cosx(2)$ $=(2x^{2}-x)-2cosx-2xsinx+sinx+2cosx$ $=2x^{2}-x-2xsinx+sinx$ $=2x(x-sinx)-1(x-sinx)$ $f^{'}(x)=(2x-1)(x-sinx)$ for $x>0,x-sinx>0$ $x<0,x-sinx<0$ for $x \in (-\infty,0]∪[\frac{1}{2},\infty),f^{'}(x) \ge 0$ for $x \in [0,\frac{1}{2}],f^{'}(x) \le 0$ Hence, f(x) increases in $[\frac{1}{2},\infty)$ .
questions.explanation_html:
Given, $f(x)=\frac{4x^{3}-3x^{2}}{6}-2sinx+(2x-1)cosx$

$f^{'}(x)=\frac{12x^{2}-6x}{6}-2cosx+(2x-1)(-sinx)+cosx(2)$

$=(2x^{2}-x)-2cosx-2xsinx+sinx+2cosx$

$=2x^{2}-x-2xsinx+sinx$

$=2x(x-sinx)-1(x-sinx)$

$f^{'}(x)=(2x-1)(x-sinx)$

for $x>0,x-sinx>0$

$x<0,x-sinx<0$

for $x \in (-\infty,0]∪[\frac{1}{2},\infty),f^{'}(x) \ge 0$

for $x \in [0,\frac{1}{2}],f^{'}(x) \le 0$

Hence, f(x) increases in $[\frac{1}{2},\infty)$ .

questions.question_text: The number of distinct real roots of the equation 3x 4 + 4x 3 $-$ 12x 2 + 4 = 0 is _____________.
questions.question_html: The number of distinct real roots of the equation 3x4 + 4x3 $-$ 12x2 + 4 = 0 is _____________.
questions.explanation_text: 3x 4 + 4x 3 $-$ 12x 2 + 4 = 0 So, let f(x) = 3x 4 + 4x 3 $-$ 12x 2 + 4 $\therefore$ f'(x) = 12x(x 2 + x $-$ 2) = 12x (x + 2) (x $-$ 1) $\therefore$ f'(x) = 12x 3 + 12x 2 – 24x = 12x(x + 2) (x – 1) Points of extrema are at x = 0, –2, 1 f(0) = 4 f(–2) = –28 f(1) = –1 So, 4 Real Roots
questions.explanation_html:
3x4 + 4x3 $-$ 12x2 + 4 = 0

So, let f(x) = 3x4 + 4x3 $-$ 12x2 + 4

$\therefore$ f'(x) = 12x(x2 + x $-$ 2)

= 12x (x + 2) (x $-$ 1)

$\therefore$ f'(x) = 12x3 + 12x2 – 24x = 12x(x + 2) (x – 1)

Points of extrema are at x = 0, –2, 1

f(0) = 4

f(1) = –1

So, 4 Real Roots

questions.question_html:
Let a be an integer such that all the real roots of the polynomial
2x5 + 5x4 + 10x3 + 10x2 + 10x + 10 lie in the interval (a, a + 1). Then, |a| is equal to ___________.
questions.explanation_text: Let, $f(x)=2x^{5}+5x^{4}+10x^{3}+10x^{2}+10x+10$ $\Rightarrow f^{'}(x)=10(x^{4}+2x^{3}+3x^{2}+2x+1)$ $=10(x^{2}+\frac{1}{x^{2}}+2(x+\frac{1}{x})+3)$ $=10((x+\frac{1}{x})^{2}+2(x+\frac{1}{x})+1)$ $=10((x+\frac{1}{x})+1)^{2}>0;∀x \in R$ $\therefore$ f(x) is strictly increasing function. Since, it is an odd degree polynomial it will have exactly one real root. Now, by observation. $f(-1)=3>0$ $f(-2)=-64+80-80+40-20+10$ $=-34<0$ $\Rightarrow f(x)$ has at least one root in $(-2,-1) \equiv (a,a+1)$ $\Rightarrow a=-2$ $\Rightarrow$ |a| = - 2
questions.explanation_html:
Let, $f(x)=2x^{5}+5x^{4}+10x^{3}+10x^{2}+10x+10$

$\Rightarrow f^{'}(x)=10(x^{4}+2x^{3}+3x^{2}+2x+1)$

$=10(x^{2}+\frac{1}{x^{2}}+2(x+\frac{1}{x})+3)$

$=10((x+\frac{1}{x})^{2}+2(x+\frac{1}{x})+1)$

$=10((x+\frac{1}{x})+1)^{2}>0;∀x \in R$

$\therefore$ f(x) is strictly increasing function. Since, it is an odd degree polynomial it will have exactly one real root.

Now, by observation.

$f(-1)=3>0$

$f(-2)=-64+80-80+40-20+10$

$=-34<0$

$\Rightarrow f(x)$ has at least one root in $(-2,-1) \equiv (a,a+1)$

$\Rightarrow a=-2$

$\Rightarrow$ |a| = - 2

questions.question_html: A box open from top is made from a rectangular sheet of dimension a $\times$ b by cutting squares each of side x from each of the four corners and folding up the flaps. If the volume of the box is maximum, then x is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: V = l . b . h = (a $-$ 2x)(b $-$ 2x) x $\Rightarrow$ V(x) = (2x $-$ a)(2x $-$ b) x $\Rightarrow$ V(x) = 4x 3 $-$ 2(a + b)x 2 + abx $\Rightarrow \frac{d}{dx}v(x)=12x^{2}-4(a+b)x+ab$ $\frac{d}{dx}(v(x))=0 \Rightarrow 12x^{2}-4(a+b)x+ab=0<_{\beta}^{\alpha}$ $\Rightarrow x=\frac{4(a+b) \pm \sqrt{16(a+b)^{2}-48ab}}{2(12)}$ $=\frac{(a+b) \pm \sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}-ab}}{6}$ Let $x=\alpha=\frac{(a+b)+\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}-ab}}{6}$ $\beta=\frac{(a+b)-\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}-ab}}{6}$ Now, $12(x-\alpha)(x-\beta)=0$ $\therefore$ x = $\beta$ $=\frac{a+b-\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}-ab}}{b}$

questions.question_text: Let f : R $\rightarrow$ R be defined as $f(x)={\begin{aligned} -\frac{4}{3}x^{3}+2x^{2}+3x, & x>0 \\ 3xe^{x}, & x \le 0 \end{aligned}$ . Then f is increasing function in the interval
questions.question_html:
Let f : R $\rightarrow$ R be defined as

$f(x)={\begin{aligned} -\frac{4}{3}x^{3}+2x^{2}+3x, & x>0 \\ 3xe^{x}, & x \le 0 \end{aligned}$ . Then f is increasing function in the interval
questions.explanation_text: $f^{'}(x){\begin{aligned} -4x^{2}+4x+3 & x>0 \\ 3e^{x}(1+x) & x \le 0 \end{aligned}$ For x > 0, $f^{'}(x)=-4x^{2}+4x+3$ f(x) is increasing in $(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2})$ For x $\le$ 0, f'(x) = 3e x (1 + x) f'(x) > 0 $∀$ x $\in$ ( $-$ 1, 0) $\Rightarrow$ f(x) is increasing in ( $-$ 1, 0) So, in complete domain, f(x) is increasing in $(-1,\frac{3}{2})$
questions.explanation_html:
$f^{'}(x){\begin{aligned} -4x^{2}+4x+3 & x>0 \\ 3e^{x}(1+x) & x \le 0 \end{aligned}$


For x > 0, $f^{'}(x)=-4x^{2}+4x+3$

f(x) is increasing in $(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2})$

For x $\le$ 0, f'(x) = 3ex(1 + x)

f'(x) > 0 $∀$ x $\in$ ( $-$ 1, 0)

$\Rightarrow$ f(x) is increasing in ( $-$ 1, 0)

So, in complete domain, f(x) is increasing in $(-1,\frac{3}{2})$

questions.question_html: The maximum slope of the curve $y=\frac{1}{2}x^{4}-5x^{3}+18x^{2}-19x$ occurs at the point :
questions.explanation_text: Given, $y=\frac{1}{2}x^{4}-5x^{3}+18x^{2}-19x$ $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{2} \times 4x^{3}-15x^{2}+36x-19$ $\Rightarrow$ Slope M = $2x^{3}-15x^{2}+36x-19$ At max of slope $\frac{dM}{dx}=0$ $\therefore$ $\frac{dM}{dx}=6x^{2}-30x+36=0$ $\Rightarrow 6(x^{2}-5x+6)=0$ $\Rightarrow 6(x-2)(x-3)=0$ $\therefore$ $x=2,3$ Now, $\frac{d^{2}M}{dx^{2}}=6(2x-5)$ at $x=2,\frac{d^{2}M}{dx^{2}}=6(4-5)=-6<0$ $\therefore$ at x = 2 slope is maximum. At x = 2, y = 8 - 40 + 72 - 38 = 2 $\therefore$ Required point = (2, 2)
questions.explanation_html:
Given, $y=\frac{1}{2}x^{4}-5x^{3}+18x^{2}-19x$

$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{2} \times 4x^{3}-15x^{2}+36x-19$

$\Rightarrow$ Slope M = $2x^{3}-15x^{2}+36x-19$

At max of slope $\frac{dM}{dx}=0$

$\therefore$ $\frac{dM}{dx}=6x^{2}-30x+36=0$

$\Rightarrow 6(x^{2}-5x+6)=0$

$\Rightarrow 6(x-2)(x-3)=0$

$\therefore$ $x=2,3$

Now, $\frac{d^{2}M}{dx^{2}}=6(2x-5)$

at $x=2,\frac{d^{2}M}{dx^{2}}=6(4-5)=-6<0$

$\therefore$ at x = 2 slope is maximum.

At x = 2,

y = 8 - 40 + 72 - 38 = 2

$\therefore$ Required point = (2, 2)

If the tangent to the curve y = x 3 at the point P(t, t 3 ) meets the curve again at Q, then the
ordinate of the point which divides PQ internally in the ratio 1 : 2 is :
questions.question_html: If the tangent to the curve y = x3 at the point P(t, t3) meets the curve again at Q, then the ordinate of the point which divides PQ internally in the ratio 1 : 2 is :
questions.explanation_text: Given $P(t,t^{3})$ Let $Q=(t_{1},t_{1}^{3})$ Slope of tangent at point p, $\frac{dy}{dx}=3x^{2}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}|_{(t,t^{3})}=3t^{2}$ This slope is same as slope of line PQ. Slope of $PQ=\frac{t_{1}^{3}-t_{3}}{t_{1}-t}$ $\therefore$ $3t^{2}=\frac{t_{1}^{3}-t_{3}}{t_{1}-t}$ $\Rightarrow 3t^{2}=\frac{(t_{1}-t)(t_{1}^{2}+tt_{1}+t^{2})}{(t_{1}-t)}$ $\Rightarrow 3t^{2}=t_{1}^{2}+tt_{1}+t^{2}$ $\Rightarrow t_{1}=-2t$ $\therefore$ $Q=(-2t,-8t^{3})$ $\therefore$ $ℎ=\frac{2t-2t}{3}=0$ $k=\frac{2t^{3}-8t^{3}}{3}=-2t^{3}$ $\therefore$ Point $M=(0,-2t^{3})$
questions.explanation_html:
Given $P(t,t^{3})$

Let $Q=(t_{1},t_{1}^{3})$

Slope of tangent at point p,

$\frac{dy}{dx}=3x^{2}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}|_{(t,t^{3})}=3t^{2}$

This slope is same as slope of line PQ.

Slope of $PQ=\frac{t_{1}^{3}-t_{3}}{t_{1}-t}$

$\therefore$ $3t^{2}=\frac{t_{1}^{3}-t_{3}}{t_{1}-t}$

$\Rightarrow 3t^{2}=\frac{(t_{1}-t)(t_{1}^{2}+tt_{1}+t^{2})}{(t_{1}-t)}$

$\Rightarrow 3t^{2}=t_{1}^{2}+tt_{1}+t^{2}$

$\Rightarrow t_{1}=-2t$

$\therefore$ $Q=(-2t,-8t^{3})$



$\therefore$ $ℎ=\frac{2t-2t}{3}=0$

$k=\frac{2t^{3}-8t^{3}}{3}=-2t^{3}$

$\therefore$ Point $M=(0,-2t^{3})$

questions.question_text: A wire of length 36 m is cut into two pieces, one of the pieces is bent to form a square and the other is bent to form a circle. If the sum of the areas of the two figures is minimum, and the circumference of the circle is k (meter), then $(\frac{4}{\pi}+1)k$ is equal to _____________.
questions.question_html: A wire of length 36 m is cut into two pieces, one of the pieces is bent to form a square and the other is bent to form a circle. If the sum of the areas of the two figures is minimum, and the circumference of the circle is k (meter), then $(\frac{4}{\pi}+1)k$ is equal to _____________.
questions.explanation_text: Let x + y = 36 x is perimeter of square and y is perimeter of circle side of square = x/4 radius of circle = $\frac{y}{2\pi}$ Sum Areas = $(\frac{x}{4})^{2}+\pi(\frac{y}{2\pi})^{2}$ $=\frac{x^{2}}{16}+\frac{(36-x)^{2}}{4\pi}$ For min Area : $x=\frac{144}{\pi+4}$ $\Rightarrow$ Radius = y = 36 $-$ $\frac{144}{\pi+4}$ $\Rightarrow$ k = $\frac{36\pi}{\pi+4}$ $(\frac{4}{\pi}+1)k$ = 36
questions.explanation_html:
Let x + y = 36

x is perimeter of square and y is perimeter of circle side of square = x/4

radius of circle = $\frac{y}{2\pi}$

Sum Areas = $(\frac{x}{4})^{2}+\pi(\frac{y}{2\pi})^{2}$

$=\frac{x^{2}}{16}+\frac{(36-x)^{2}}{4\pi}$

For min Area :

$x=\frac{144}{\pi+4}$

$\Rightarrow$ Radius = y = 36 $-$ $\frac{144}{\pi+4}$

$\Rightarrow$ k = $\frac{36\pi}{\pi+4}$

$(\frac{4}{\pi}+1)k$ = 36

questions.question_html: If the curves x = y4 and xy = k cut at right angles, then (4k)6 is equal to __________.
questions.explanation_text: $x=y^{4}$ and $xy=k$ for intersection $y^{5}=k$ ..... (1) Also $x=y^{4}$ $\Rightarrow 1=4y^{3}\frac{dy}{dx} \Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{4y^{3}}$ for $xy=k \Rightarrow x=\frac{k}{y}$ $\Rightarrow 1=-\frac{k}{y^{2}}.\frac{dy}{dx}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-y^{2}}{k}$ $\because$ Curve cut orthogonally $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{4y^{3}} \times (\frac{-y^{2}}{k})=-1$ $\Rightarrow y=\frac{1}{4k}$ $\therefore$ from (1), $y^{5}=k$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{(4k)^{5}}=k$ $\Rightarrow 4=(4k)^{6}$
questions.explanation_html:
$x=y^{4}$ and $xy=k$

for intersection $y^{5}=k$ ..... (1)

Also $x=y^{4}$

$\Rightarrow 1=4y^{3}\frac{dy}{dx} \Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{4y^{3}}$

for $xy=k \Rightarrow x=\frac{k}{y}$

$\Rightarrow 1=-\frac{k}{y^{2}}.\frac{dy}{dx}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-y^{2}}{k}$

$\because$ Curve cut orthogonally

$\Rightarrow \frac{1}{4y^{3}} \times (\frac{-y^{2}}{k})=-1$

$\Rightarrow y=\frac{1}{4k}$

$\therefore$ from (1), $y^{5}=k$

$\Rightarrow \frac{1}{(4k)^{5}}=k$

$\Rightarrow 4=(4k)^{6}$

questions.question_html:
Let the normal at a point P on the curve
y2 – 3x2 + y + 10 = 0 intersect the y-axis at $(0,\frac{3}{2})$ .
If m is the slope of the tangent at P to the curve, then |m| is equal to
questions.explanation_text: Given curve : y 2 – 3x 2 + y + 10 = 0 $\Rightarrow$ 2y $\frac{dy}{dx}$ - 6x + $\frac{dy}{dx}$ = 0 $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{dy}{dx}$ = $\frac{6x}{2y+1}$ Let P be (x 1 , y 1 ) Slope of tangent at P = $\frac{6x_{1}}{2y_{1}+1}$ $\therefore$ Slope of normal at P = $-\frac{2y_{1}+1}{6x_{1}}$ $\Rightarrow$ Equation of normal (y – y 1 ) = $-(\frac{2y_{1}+1}{6x_{1}})$ (x – x 1 ) This normal passes through point $(0,\frac{3}{2})$ . $\therefore$ ( $\frac{3}{2}$ – y 1 ) = $-(\frac{2y_{1}+1}{6x_{1}})$ (0 – x 1 ) $\Rightarrow$ y 1 = 1 Put y 1 = 1 in equation of curve , then we get x 1 = $\pm$ 2 $\Rightarrow$ |m| = slope of tangent = $|\frac{6x_{1}}{2y_{1}+1}|$ = $\frac{12}{3}$ = 4
questions.explanation_html:
Given curve : y2 – 3x2 + y + 10 = 0

$\Rightarrow$ 2y $\frac{dy}{dx}$ - 6x + $\frac{dy}{dx}$ = 0

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{dy}{dx}$ = $\frac{6x}{2y+1}$

Let P be (x1, y1)

Slope of tangent at P = $\frac{6x_{1}}{2y_{1}+1}$

$\therefore$ Slope of normal at P = $-\frac{2y_{1}+1}{6x_{1}}$

$\Rightarrow$ Equation of normal (y – y1) = $-(\frac{2y_{1}+1}{6x_{1}})$ (x – x1)

This normal passes through point $(0,\frac{3}{2})$ .

$\therefore$ ( $\frac{3}{2}$ – y1) = $-(\frac{2y_{1}+1}{6x_{1}})$ (0 – x1)

$\Rightarrow$ y1 = 1

Put y1 = 1 in equation of curve , then we get x1 = $\pm$ 2

$\Rightarrow$ |m| = slope of tangent = $|\frac{6x_{1}}{2y_{1}+1}|$ = $\frac{12}{3}$ = 4

questions.question_text:
The set of all real values of $\lambda$ for which the
function $f(x)=(1-cos^{2}x)(\lambda+sinx),x \in (-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2})$ has exactly one maxima and exactly one
minima, is :
questions.question_html:
The set of all real values of $\lambda$ for which the function

$f(x)=(1-cos^{2}x)(\lambda+sinx),x \in (-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2})$

has exactly one maxima and exactly one minima, is :
questions.explanation_text: $f(x)=(1-cos^{2}x)(\lambda+sinx)$ $\Rightarrow$ f(x) = sin 2 x( $\lambda$ + sinx) ....(1) $\therefore$ f'(x) = 2sinx cosx ( $\lambda$ +sinx) + sin 2 x (cosx) $\Rightarrow$ f'(x) = sin2x( $\frac{2\lambda+3sinx}{2}$ ) For maixma and minima, f'(x) = 0 $\therefore$ sin2x = 0 or 2 $\lambda$ + 3sinx = 0 when sin2x = 0 $\Rightarrow$ x = 0 or when 2 $\lambda$ + 3sinx = 0 $\Rightarrow$ sin x = $-\frac{2\lambda}{3}$ As $x \in (-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2})$ $\therefore$ -1 < sinx < 1 $\Rightarrow$ -1 < $-\frac{2\lambda}{3}$ < 1 $\Rightarrow$ $-\frac{3}{2}$ < $\lambda$ < $\frac{3}{2}$ $\therefore$ $\lambda$ $\in$ $(-\frac{3}{2},\frac{3}{2})$ - {0} Note : If $\lambda$ = 0 $\Rightarrow$ f(x) = sin 3 x [from (1)] Which is monotonic. so no maxima/minima.
questions.explanation_html:
$f(x)=(1-cos^{2}x)(\lambda+sinx)$

$\Rightarrow$ f(x) = sin2 x( $\lambda$ + sinx) ....(1)

$\therefore$ f'(x) = 2sinx cosx ( $\lambda$ +sinx) + sin2x (cosx)

$\Rightarrow$ f'(x) = sin2x( $\frac{2\lambda+3sinx}{2}$ )

For maixma and minima, f'(x) = 0

$\therefore$ sin2x = 0 or 2 $\lambda$ + 3sinx = 0

when sin2x = 0 $\Rightarrow$ x = 0

or when 2 $\lambda$ + 3sinx = 0

$\Rightarrow$ sin x = $-\frac{2\lambda}{3}$

As $x \in (-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2})$

$\therefore$ -1 < sinx < 1

$\Rightarrow$ -1 < $-\frac{2\lambda}{3}$ < 1

$\Rightarrow$ $-\frac{3}{2}$ < $\lambda$ < $\frac{3}{2}$

$\therefore$ $\lambda$ $\in$ $(-\frac{3}{2},\frac{3}{2})$ - {0}

Note : If $\lambda$ = 0 $\Rightarrow$ f(x) = sin3x [from (1)]

Which is monotonic. so no maxima/minima.

questions.question_html: Let the function, ƒ:[-7, 0] $\rightarrow$ R be continuous on [-7,0] and differentiable on (-7, 0). If ƒ(-7) = - 3 and ƒ'(x) $\le$ 2, for all x $\in$ (-7,0), then for all such functions ƒ, ƒ(-1) + ƒ(0) lies in the interval:
questions.explanation_text: Using Lagrange’s Mean Value Theorem in [–7, –1] $\frac{f(-1)-f(-7)}{-1-(-7)}$ = f'(c 1 ) As ƒ'(x) $\le$ 2 then f'(c 1 ) $\le$ 2 $\therefore$ $\frac{f(-1)-f(-7)}{-1-(-7)}$ $\le$ 2 $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{f(-1)+3}{6}$ $\le$ 2 $\Rightarrow$ f(-1) $\le$ 9 Using Lagrange’s Mean Value Theorem in [–7, 0] $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{f(0)-f(-7)}{0-(-7)}$ $\le$ 2 $\Rightarrow$ f(0) $\le$ 11 $\therefore$ ƒ(-1) + ƒ(0) $\le$ 11 + 9 $\Rightarrow$ ƒ(-1) + ƒ(0) $\le$ 20
questions.explanation_html:
Using Lagrange’s Mean Value Theorem in [–7, –1]

$\frac{f(-1)-f(-7)}{-1-(-7)}$ = f'(c1)

As ƒ'(x) $\le$ 2 then f'(c1) $\le$ 2

$\therefore$ $\frac{f(-1)-f(-7)}{-1-(-7)}$ $\le$ 2

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{f(-1)+3}{6}$ $\le$ 2

$\Rightarrow$ f(-1) $\le$ 9

Using Lagrange’s Mean Value Theorem in [–7, 0]

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{f(0)-f(-7)}{0-(-7)}$ $\le$ 2

$\Rightarrow$ f(0) $\le$ 11

$\therefore$ ƒ(-1) + ƒ(0) $\le$ 11 + 9

$\Rightarrow$ ƒ(-1) + ƒ(0) $\le$ 20

questions.question_text: The equation of the normal to the curve y = (1+x) 2y + cos 2 (sin –1 x) at x = 0 is :
questions.question_html:
The equation of the normal to the curve
y = (1+x)2y + cos 2(sin–1x) at x = 0 is :
questions.explanation_text: Given equation of curve y = (1+x) 2y + cos 2 (sin –1 x) at x = 0 $\Rightarrow$ y = (1 + 0) 2y + cos 2 (sin –1 0) $\Rightarrow$ y = 1 + 1 $\Rightarrow$ y = 2 So we have to find the normal at (0, 2) Now, y = $e^{2yln(1+x)}+cos^{2}(cos^{-1}\sqrt{1-x^{2}})$ $\Rightarrow$ y = $e^{2yln(1+x)}+(\sqrt{1-x^{2}})^{2}$ $\Rightarrow$ y = $e^{2yln(1+x)}+(1-x^{2})$ Now differentiate w.r.t. x y' = $e^{2yln(1+x)}[2y.(\frac{1}{1+x})+ln(1+x).2y^{'}]$ - 2x Put x = 0 & y = 2 $\Rightarrow$ y' = $e^{2yln(1+0)}[2y.(\frac{1}{1+0})+ln(1+0).2y^{'}]-2 \times 0$ $\Rightarrow$ y' = e 0 [4 + 0] – 0 $\Rightarrow$ y' = 4 = slope of tangent to the curve so slope of normal to the curve = - $\frac{1}{4}$ Hence equation of normal at (0, 2) is y - 2 = - $\frac{1}{4}$ (x - 0) $\Rightarrow$ 4y – 8 = –x $\Rightarrow$ x + 4y = 8
questions.explanation_html:
Given equation of curve

y = (1+x)2y + cos 2(sin–1x)

at x = 0

$\Rightarrow$ y = (1 + 0)2y + cos2(sin–10)

$\Rightarrow$ y = 1 + 1

$\Rightarrow$ y = 2

So we have to find the normal at (0, 2)

Now, y = $e^{2yln(1+x)}+cos^{2}(cos^{-1}\sqrt{1-x^{2}})$

$\Rightarrow$ y = $e^{2yln(1+x)}+(\sqrt{1-x^{2}})^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ y = $e^{2yln(1+x)}+(1-x^{2})$

Now differentiate w.r.t. x

y' = $e^{2yln(1+x)}[2y.(\frac{1}{1+x})+ln(1+x).2y^{'}]$ - 2x

Put x = 0 & y = 2

$\Rightarrow$ y' = $e^{2yln(1+0)}[2y.(\frac{1}{1+0})+ln(1+0).2y^{'}]-2 \times 0$

$\Rightarrow$ y' = e0 [4 + 0] – 0

$\Rightarrow$ y' = 4 = slope of tangent to the curve

so slope of normal to the curve = - $\frac{1}{4}$

Hence equation of normal at (0, 2) is

y - 2 = - $\frac{1}{4}$ (x - 0)

$\Rightarrow$ 4y – 8 = –x

$\Rightarrow$ x + 4y = 8

If p(x) be a polynomial of degree three that has
a local maximum value 8 at x = 1 and a local
minimum value 4 at x = 2; then p(0) is equal to :
questions.question_html: If p(x) be a polynomial of degree three that has a local maximum value 8 at x = 1 and a local minimum value 4 at x = 2; then p(0) is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Since p(x) has relative extreme at x = 1 & 2 so p'(x) = 0 at x = 1 & 2 $\therefore$ Let p'(x) = A(x – 1) (x – 2) $\Rightarrow$ p(x) = $\int A(x^{2}-3x+2)dx$ $\Rightarrow$ p(x) = $A(\frac{x^{2}}{3}-3x^{2}+2x)$ + C ...(1) As P(1) = 8 From (1) $8=A(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{3}{2}+2)+C$ $\Rightarrow$ 8 = $\frac{5A}{6}+C$ $\Rightarrow$ 48 = 5A + 5C ...(2) Also P(2) = 4 From (1) $4=A(\frac{8}{3}-6+4)+C$ $\Rightarrow$ 4 = $\frac{2A}{3}+C$ $\Rightarrow$ 12 = 2A + 3C ......(3) Form (3) & (4), C = –12, A = 24 Now p(0) = C = -12

Since p(x) has relative extreme at

x = 1 & 2

so p'(x) = 0 at x = 1 & 2

$\therefore$ Let p'(x) = A(x – 1) (x – 2)

$\Rightarrow$ p(x) = $\int A(x^{2}-3x+2)dx$

$\Rightarrow$ p(x) = $A(\frac{x^{2}}{3}-3x^{2}+2x)$ + C ...(1)

As P(1) = 8

From (1)

$8=A(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{3}{2}+2)+C$

$\Rightarrow$ 8 = $\frac{5A}{6}+C$

$\Rightarrow$ 48 = 5A + 5C ...(2)

Also P(2) = 4

From (1)

$4=A(\frac{8}{3}-6+4)+C$

$\Rightarrow$ 4 = $\frac{2A}{3}+C$

$\Rightarrow$ 12 = 2A + 3C ......(3)

Form (3) & (4), C = –12, A = 24

Now p(0) = C = -12

$=-log_{e}(1+x)$

Let f(x) = ax 3 + bx 2 + cx + d Given f(-1) = 10, f(1) = -6 $\therefore$ -a + b - c + d = 10 ....(i) and a + b + c + d = -6 ......(ii) adding (i) + (ii) 2(b + d) = 4 $\Rightarrow$ b + d = 2 ....(iii) f'(x) = 3ax 2 + 2bx + c Given f'(-1) = 0 $\Rightarrow$ 3a - 2b + c = 0 .....(iv) f"(x) = 6ax + 2b Given f"(1) = 0 $\therefore$ 6a + 2b = 0 ....(v) $\Rightarrow$ b = -3a adding (iv) + (v), we get 9a + c = 0 ....(vi) $\Rightarrow$ $9(\frac{-b}{3})$ + c = 0 $\Rightarrow$ c = 3b f(x) = $\frac{-b}{3}x^{3}$ + bx 2 + 3bx + (2 - b) $\Rightarrow$ f'(x) = -bx 2 + 2bx + 3b = -b(x 2 - 2x - 3) At maxima and minima f'(x) = 0 $\therefore$ (x 2 - 2x - 3) = 0 $\Rightarrow$ (x - 3) (x + 1) = 0 x = 3, -1 As a + b + c + d = -6 $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{-b}{3}$ + b + 3b + 2 - b = -6 $\Rightarrow$ b = -3 $\therefore$ f'(x) = 3(x 2 - 2x - 3) $\Rightarrow$ f''(x) = 3(2x
 - 2) At x = 3, f''(x) = 3(2.3
 - 2) = 12 > 0 $\therefore$ Minima
at x = 3.
questions.explanation_html:
Let f(x) = ax3 + bx2 + cx + d

Given f(-1) = 10, f(1) = -6

$\therefore$ -a + b - c + d = 10 ....(i)

and a + b + c + d = -6 ......(ii)

adding (i) + (ii)

2(b + d) = 4

$\Rightarrow$ b + d = 2 ....(iii)

f'(x) = 3ax2 + 2bx + c

Given f'(-1) = 0

$\Rightarrow$ 3a - 2b + c = 0 .....(iv)

f"(x) = 6ax + 2b

Given f"(1) = 0

$\therefore$ 6a + 2b = 0 ....(v)

$\Rightarrow$ b = -3a

adding (iv) + (v), we get

9a + c = 0 ....(vi)

$\Rightarrow$ $9(\frac{-b}{3})$ + c = 0

$\Rightarrow$ c = 3b

f(x) = $\frac{-b}{3}x^{3}$ + bx2 + 3bx + (2 - b)

$\Rightarrow$ f'(x) = -bx2 + 2bx + 3b

= -b(x2 - 2x - 3)

At maxima and minima f'(x) = 0

$\therefore$ (x2 - 2x - 3) = 0

$\Rightarrow$ (x - 3) (x + 1) = 0

x = 3, -1

As a + b + c + d = -6

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{-b}{3}$ + b + 3b + 2 - b = -6

$\Rightarrow$ b = -3

$\therefore$ f'(x) = 3(x2 - 2x - 3)

$\Rightarrow$ f''(x) = 3(2x - 2)

At x = 3, f''(x) = 3(2.3 - 2) = 12 > 0

$\therefore$ Minima at x = 3.

questions.question_html: Let ƒ : [0, 2] $\rightarrow$ R be a twice differentiable function such that ƒ''(x) > 0, for all x $\in$ (0, 2). If $\phi$ (x) = ƒ(x) + ƒ(2 – x), then $\phi$ is :

options.label: B
