questions.explanation_text: $\phi$ (x) = ƒ(x) + ƒ(2 – x) $\Rightarrow$ $\phi$ '(x) = ƒ'(x) - ƒ'(2 – x) Since ƒ''(x) > 0 for all x $\in$ (0, 2) $\Rightarrow$ ƒ'(x) is an increasing function for all x $\in$ (0, 2). Case 1 : When $\phi$ (x) is increasing function So $\phi$ '(x) > 0 $\Rightarrow$ ƒ'(x) - ƒ'(2 – x) > 0 $\Rightarrow$ ƒ'(x) > ƒ'(2 – x) $\Rightarrow$ x > 2 – x $\Rightarrow$ x > 1 $\therefore$ $\phi$ (x) is increasing on (1, 2). Case 2 : When $\phi$ (x) is decreasing function So $\phi$ '(x) < 0 $\Rightarrow$ ƒ'(x) - ƒ'(2 – x) < 0 $\Rightarrow$ ƒ'(x) < ƒ'(2 – x) $\Rightarrow$ x < 2 – x $\Rightarrow$ x < 1 $\therefore$ $\phi$ (x) is decreasing on (0, 1).
questions.explanation_html:
$\phi$ (x) = ƒ(x) + ƒ(2 – x)

$\Rightarrow$ $\phi$ '(x) = ƒ'(x) - ƒ'(2 – x)

Since ƒ''(x) > 0 for all x $\in$ (0, 2)

$\Rightarrow$ ƒ'(x) is an increasing function for all x $\in$ (0, 2).

Case 1 : When $\phi$ (x) is increasing function

So $\phi$ '(x) > 0

$\Rightarrow$ ƒ'(x) - ƒ'(2 – x) > 0

$\Rightarrow$ ƒ'(x) > ƒ'(2 – x)

$\Rightarrow$ x > 2 – x

$\Rightarrow$ x > 1

$\therefore$ $\phi$ (x) is increasing on (1, 2).

Case 2 : When $\phi$ (x) is decreasing function

So $\phi$ '(x) < 0

$\Rightarrow$ ƒ'(x) - ƒ'(2 – x) < 0

$\Rightarrow$ ƒ'(x) < ƒ'(2 – x)

$\Rightarrow$ x < 2 – x

$\Rightarrow$ x < 1

$\therefore$ $\phi$ (x) is decreasing on (0, 1).

questions.explanation_text: $f(x)=x\sqrt{kx-x^{2}}$ $\Rightarrow$ $f^{'}(x)=\sqrt{kx-x^{2}}+\frac{(k-2x)x}{2\sqrt{kx-x^{2}}}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{2(kx-x^{2})+kx-2x^{2}}{2\sqrt{kx-x^{2}}}=\frac{3kx-4x^{2}}{2\sqrt{kx-x^{2}}}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{x(3k-4x)}{2\sqrt{kx-x^{2}}}$ Now for increasing function for f'(x) $\ge$ 0, $∀x \in [0,3]$ $\Rightarrow kx-x^{2} \ge 0,∀x \in [0,3]andx(3k-4x) \ge 0,∀x \in [0,3]$ $\Rightarrow x(x-k) \le 0,∀x \in [0,3]andx(4x-3k) \le 0,∀x \in [0,3]$ k $\ge$ 3 and k $\ge$ 4 $\Rightarrow$ k $\ge$ 4 $\Rightarrow$ m = 4 So f(x) is maximum when k = 4 then $3\sqrt{4 \times 3-3^{2}}=3\sqrt{3}=M$ $\therefore$ (m, M) = (4, $3\sqrt{3}$ )

Now for increasing function

questions.explanation_text: To determine the absolute maximum (M) and absolute minimum (m) of the function $f(x)=2x^{3}-9x^{2}+12x+5$ over the interval $[0,3]$ , we need to examine its critical points and endpoints. First, we find the derivative of the function, $f^{'}(x)$ , to locate the critical points: $f^{'}(x)=\frac{d}{dx}(2x^{3}-9x^{2}+12x+5)=6x^{2}-18x+12$ Next, we set the derivative equal to zero to find the critical points: $6x^{2}-18x+12=0$ Simplifying this equation by dividing by 6: $x^{2}-3x+2=0$ We solve this quadratic equation using the factorization method: $(x-1)(x-2)=0$ So, the critical points are: $x=1\text{and}x=2$ We now evaluate the function $f(x)$ at the critical points and at the endpoints of the interval [0, 3]: 1. At $x=0$ : $f(0)=2(0)^{3}-9(0)^{2}+12(0)+5=5$ 2. At $x=1$ : $f(1)=2(1)^{3}-9(1)^{2}+12(1)+5=2-9+12+5=10$ 3. At $x=2$ : $f(2)=2(2)^{3}-9(2)^{2}+12(2)+5=16-36+24+5=9$ 4. At $x=3$ : $f(3)=2(3)^{3}-9(3)^{2}+12(3)+5=54-81+36+5=14$ We now identify the absolute maximum (M) and absolute minimum (m) from the above values: Maximum value $M=14$ at $x=3$ Minimum value $m=5$ at $x=0$ Thus, the difference $M-m$ is: $M-m=14-5=9$ Therefore, the correct answer is: Option B: 9
questions.explanation_html:
To determine the absolute maximum (M) and absolute minimum (m) of the function $f(x)=2x^{3}-9x^{2}+12x+5$ over the interval $[0,3]$ , we need to examine its critical points and endpoints.

First, we find the derivative of the function, $f^{'}(x)$ , to locate the critical points:

$f^{'}(x)=\frac{d}{dx}(2x^{3}-9x^{2}+12x+5)=6x^{2}-18x+12$

Next, we set the derivative equal to zero to find the critical points:

$6x^{2}-18x+12=0$

Simplifying this equation by dividing by 6:

$x^{2}-3x+2=0$

We solve this quadratic equation using the factorization method:

$(x-1)(x-2)=0$

So, the critical points are:

$x=1\text{and}x=2$

We now evaluate the function $f(x)$ at the critical points and at the endpoints of the interval [0, 3]:

1. At $x=0$ :

$f(0)=2(0)^{3}-9(0)^{2}+12(0)+5=5$

2. At $x=1$ :

$f(1)=2(1)^{3}-9(1)^{2}+12(1)+5=2-9+12+5=10$

3. At $x=2$ :

$f(2)=2(2)^{3}-9(2)^{2}+12(2)+5=16-36+24+5=9$

4. At $x=3$ :

$f(3)=2(3)^{3}-9(3)^{2}+12(3)+5=54-81+36+5=14$

We now identify the absolute maximum (M) and absolute minimum (m) from the above values:

  • Maximum value $M=14$ at $x=3$
  • Minimum value $m=5$ at $x=0$

Thus, the difference $M-m$ is:

$M-m=14-5=9$

Therefore, the correct answer is:

Option B: 9

At maximum or minimum $f^{'}(t)=0$ .

Min of $f(t)=\frac{(\sqrt{2})^{2}+2}{\sqrt{2}}$ = $\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}}$ = $2\sqrt{2}$

questions.question_html:
Consider :

A normal to $y=$ f $(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi}{6}$ also passes through the point:
questions.explanation_text: $f(x)=tan^{-1}(\sqrt{\frac{1+sinx}{1-sinx}})$ $=tan^{-1}(\sqrt{\frac{(sin\frac{x}{2}+cos\frac{x}{2})^{2}}{(sin\frac{x}{x}-cos\frac{x}{2})^{2}}})$ $=tan^{-1}(\frac{1+tan\frac{x}{2}}{1-tan\frac{x}{2}})$ $=tan^{-1}(tan(\frac{\pi}{4}+\frac{x}{2}))$ $\Rightarrow y=\frac{\pi}{4}+\frac{x}{2}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{2}$ Slope of normal $=\frac{-1}{(\frac{dy}{dx})}=-2$ At $(\frac{\pi}{6},\frac{\pi}{4}+\frac{\pi}{12})$ $y-(\frac{\pi}{4}+\frac{\pi}{12})=-2(x-\frac{\pi}{6})$ $y-\frac{4\pi}{12}=-2x+\frac{2\pi}{6}$ $y-\frac{\pi}{3}=-2x+\frac{\pi}{3}$ $y=-2x+\frac{2\pi}{3}$ This equation is satisfied only by the point $(0,\frac{2\pi}{3})$
questions.explanation_html:
$f(x)=tan^{-1}(\sqrt{\frac{1+sinx}{1-sinx}})$

$=tan^{-1}(\sqrt{\frac{(sin\frac{x}{2}+cos\frac{x}{2})^{2}}{(sin\frac{x}{x}-cos\frac{x}{2})^{2}}})$

$=tan^{-1}(\frac{1+tan\frac{x}{2}}{1-tan\frac{x}{2}})$

$=tan^{-1}(tan(\frac{\pi}{4}+\frac{x}{2}))$

$\Rightarrow y=\frac{\pi}{4}+\frac{x}{2}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{2}$

Slope of normal $=\frac{-1}{(\frac{dy}{dx})}=-2$

At $(\frac{\pi}{6},\frac{\pi}{4}+\frac{\pi}{12})$

$y-(\frac{\pi}{4}+\frac{\pi}{12})=-2(x-\frac{\pi}{6})$

$y-\frac{4\pi}{12}=-2x+\frac{2\pi}{6}$

$y-\frac{\pi}{3}=-2x+\frac{\pi}{3}$

$y=-2x+\frac{2\pi}{3}$

This equation is satisfied only by the point

$(0,\frac{2\pi}{3})$

questions.question_html: The minimum distance of a point on the curve y = x2−4 from the origin is :
questions.explanation_text: Let point on the curve y = x 2 $-$ 4 is ( $\alpha$ 2 , $\alpha$ 2 $-$ 4) $\therefore$ Distance of the point ( $\alpha$ 2 , $\alpha$ 2 $-$ 4) from origin, D = $\sqrt{\alpha^{2}+(\alpha^{2}-4)^{2}}$ $\Rightarrow$ D 2 = $\alpha$ 2 + $\alpha$ 4 + 16 $-$ 8 $\alpha$ 2 $=$ $\alpha$ 4 $-$ 7 $\alpha$ 2 + 16 $\therefore$ $\frac{dD^{2}}{d\alpha}$ = 4 $\alpha$ 3 $-$ 14 $\alpha$ Now, $\frac{dD^{2}}{d\alpha}$ = 0 $\Rightarrow$ 4 $\alpha$ 3 $-$ 14 $\alpha$ = 0 $\Rightarrow$ 2 $\alpha$ (2 $\alpha$ 2 $-$ 7) = 0 $\alpha$ = 0    or $\alpha$ 2 = $\frac{7}{2}$ $\frac{d^{2}D^{2}}{d\alpha^{2}}=12\alpha^{2}-14$ $\therefore$ $(\frac{d^{2}D^{2}}{d\alpha^{2}})_{at\alpha=0}=-14<0$ $(\frac{d^{2}D^{2}}{d\alpha^{2}})_{at\alpha^{2}=\frac{7}{2}}=28>0$ $\therefore$ Distance is minimum at $\alpha$ 2 = $\frac{7}{2}$ $\therefore$ Minimum distance D = $\sqrt{\frac{49}{4}-\frac{49}{4}+16}$ = $\frac{\sqrt{15}}{2}$

$\Rightarrow$    D2 = $\alpha$ 2 + $\alpha$ 4 + 16 $-$ 8 $\alpha$ 2

$=$ $\alpha$ 4 $-$ 7 $\alpha$ 2 + 16

Now, $\frac{dD^{2}}{d\alpha}$ = 0

= $\frac{\sqrt{15}}{2}$

questions.question_text: Let $f(x)$ be a polynomial of degree four having extreme values at $x=1$ and $x=2$ . If $\underset{x \rightarrow 0}{lim}[1+\frac{f(x)}{x^{2}}]=3$ , then f $(2)$ is equal to :
questions.question_html:
Let $f(x)$ be a polynomial of degree four having extreme values
at $x=1$ and $x=2$ . If $\underset{x \rightarrow 0}{lim}[1+\frac{f(x)}{x^{2}}]=3$ , then f $(2)$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: $\underset{x \rightarrow 0}{lim}[1+\frac{f(x)}{x^{2}}]=3 \Rightarrow \underset{x \rightarrow 0}{Lim}\frac{f(x)}{x^{2}}=2$ So, $f(x)$ contains terms in $x^{2},x^{3}$ and $x^{4}$ Let $f(x)=a_{1}x^{2}+a_{2}x^{3}+a_{3}x^{4}$ Since $\underset{x \rightarrow 0}{lim}\frac{f(x)}{x^{2}}=2 \Rightarrow a_{1}=2$ Hence, $f(x)=2x^{2}+a_{2}x^{3}+a_{3}x^{4}$ $f^{'}(x)=4x+3a_{2}x^{2}+4a_{3}x^{3}$ As given: $f^{'}(1)=0$ and $f^{'}(2)=0$ Hence, $4+3a_{2}+4a_{3}=0...(1)$ and $8+12a_{2}+32a_{3}=0...(1)$ By $4x(eq1)-eq(2),$ we get $16+12a_{2}+16a_{3}-(8+12a_{2}+32a_{3})=0$ $\Rightarrow 8-16a_{3}=0 \Rightarrow a_{3}=1/2$ and by eqn. $(1),4+3a_{2}+4/2=0 \Rightarrow a_{2}=-2$ $\Rightarrow f(x)=2x^{2}-2x^{3}+\frac{1}{2}x^{4}$ $f(2)=2 \times 4-2 \times 8+\frac{1}{2} \times 16=0$
questions.explanation_html:
$\underset{x \rightarrow 0}{lim}[1+\frac{f(x)}{x^{2}}]=3 \Rightarrow \underset{x \rightarrow 0}{Lim}\frac{f(x)}{x^{2}}=2$

So, $f(x)$ contains terms in $x^{2},x^{3}$ and $x^{4}$

Let $f(x)=a_{1}x^{2}+a_{2}x^{3}+a_{3}x^{4}$

Since $\underset{x \rightarrow 0}{lim}\frac{f(x)}{x^{2}}=2 \Rightarrow a_{1}=2$

Hence, $f(x)=2x^{2}+a_{2}x^{3}+a_{3}x^{4}$

$f^{'}(x)=4x+3a_{2}x^{2}+4a_{3}x^{3}$

As given: $f^{'}(1)=0$ and $f^{'}(2)=0$

Hence, $4+3a_{2}+4a_{3}=0...(1)$

and $8+12a_{2}+32a_{3}=0...(1)$

By $4x(eq1)-eq(2),$ we get

$16+12a_{2}+16a_{3}-(8+12a_{2}+32a_{3})=0$

$\Rightarrow 8-16a_{3}=0 \Rightarrow a_{3}=1/2$

and by eqn. $(1),4+3a_{2}+4/2=0 \Rightarrow a_{2}=-2$

$\Rightarrow f(x)=2x^{2}-2x^{3}+\frac{1}{2}x^{4}$

$f(2)=2 \times 4-2 \times 8+\frac{1}{2} \times 16=0$

questions.question_text: A spherical balloon is filled with $4500\pi$ cubic meters of helium gas. If a leak in the balloon causes the gas to escape at the rate of $72\pi$ cubic meters per minute, then the rate (in meters per minute) at which the radius of the balloon decreases $49$ minutes after the leakage began is :
questions.question_html: A spherical balloon is filled with $4500\pi$ cubic meters of helium gas. If a leak in the balloon causes the gas to escape at the rate of $72\pi$ cubic meters per minute, then the rate (in meters per minute) at which the radius of the balloon decreases $49$ minutes after the leakage began is :
questions.explanation_text: Volume of spherical balloon $=V=\frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}$ $\Rightarrow 4500\pi=\frac{4\pi r^{3}}{3}$ ( as Given, volume $=4500\pi m^{3}$ ) Differentiating both the sides, $w.r.t^{'}t^{'}$ we get, $\frac{dV}{dt}=4\pi r^{2}(\frac{dr}{dt})$ Now, it is given that $\frac{dV}{dt}=72\pi$ $\therefore$ After $49$ min, Volume - $=(4500-49 \times 72)\pi$ $=(4500-3528)\pi$ $=972\pi m^{3}$ $\Rightarrow V=972\pi m^{3}$ $\therefore$ $972\pi=\frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}$ $\Rightarrow r^{3}=3 \times 243=3 \times 3^{5}=3^{6}=(3^{2})^{3} \Rightarrow r=9$ Also, we have $\frac{dV}{dt}=72\pi$ $\therefore$ $72\pi=4\pi \times 9 \times 9(\frac{dr}{dt}) \Rightarrow \frac{dr}{dt}=(\frac{2}{9})$
questions.explanation_html:
Volume of spherical balloon $=V=\frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}$

$\Rightarrow 4500\pi=\frac{4\pi r^{3}}{3}$

( as Given, volume $=4500\pi m^{3}$ )

Differentiating both the sides, $w.r.t^{'}t^{'}$ we get,

$\frac{dV}{dt}=4\pi r^{2}(\frac{dr}{dt})$

Now, it is given that $\frac{dV}{dt}=72\pi$

$\therefore$ After $49$ min, Volume -

$=(4500-49 \times 72)\pi$

$=(4500-3528)\pi$

$=972\pi m^{3}$

$\Rightarrow V=972\pi m^{3}$

$\therefore$ $972\pi=\frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}$

$\Rightarrow r^{3}=3 \times 243=3 \times 3^{5}=3^{6}=(3^{2})^{3} \Rightarrow r=9$

Also, we have $\frac{dV}{dt}=72\pi$

$\therefore$ $72\pi=4\pi \times 9 \times 9(\frac{dr}{dt}) \Rightarrow \frac{dr}{dt}=(\frac{2}{9})$

questions.question_text: A line is drawn through the point $(1,2)$ to meet the coordinate axes at $P$ and $Q$ such that it forms a triangle $OPQ,$ where $O$ is the origin. If the area of the triangle $OPQ$ is least, then the slope of the line $PQ$ is :
questions.question_html: A line is drawn through the point $(1,2)$ to meet the coordinate axes at $P$ and $Q$ such that it forms a triangle $OPQ,$ where $O$ is the origin. If the area of the triangle $OPQ$ is least, then the slope of the line $PQ$ is :
questions.explanation_text: Equation of a line passing through $(x_{1},y_{1})$ having slope $m$ is given by $y-y_{1}=m(x-x_{1})$ Since the line $PQ$ is passing through $(1,2)$ therefore its equation is $(y-2)=m(x-1)$ where $m$ is the slope of the line $PQ$ . Now, point $P(x,0)$ will also satisfy the equation of $PQ$ $\therefore$ $y-2=m(x-1)$ $\Rightarrow 0-2=m(x-1)$ $\Rightarrow -2=m(x-1)$ $\Rightarrow x-1=\frac{-2}{m}$ $\Rightarrow x=\frac{-2}{m}+1$ Also, $OP=\sqrt{(x-0)^{2}+(0-0)^{2}}=x=\frac{-2}{m}+1$ Similarly, point $Q(0,y)$ will satisfy equation of $PQ$ $\therefore$ $y-2=m(x-1)$ $\Rightarrow y-2=m(-1) \Rightarrow y=2-m$ b and $OQ=y=2-m$ Area of $\Delta POQ=\frac{1}{2}(OP)(OQ)=\frac{1}{2}(1-\frac{2}{m})(2-m)$ ( As Area of $\Delta=\frac{1}{2} \times$ base $\times$ height ) $=\frac{1}{2}[2-m-\frac{4}{m}+2]=\frac{1}{2}[4-(m+\frac{4}{m})]$ $=2-\frac{m}{2}-\frac{2}{m}$ Let Area $=f(m)=2-\frac{m}{2}-\frac{2}{m}$ Now, $f^{'}(m)=\frac{-1}{2}+\frac{2}{m^{2}}$ Put $f^{'}(m)=0$ $\Rightarrow m^{2}=4 \Rightarrow m= \pm 2$ Now, $f^{''}(m)=\frac{-4}{m^{3}}$ $f^{''}(m)|_{m=2}=-\frac{1}{2}<0$ $f^{''}(m)|_{m=-2}=\frac{1}{2}>0$ Area will be least at $m=-2$ Hence, slope of $PQ$ is $-2.$
questions.explanation_html:
Equation of a line passing through $(x_{1},y_{1})$ having

slope $m$ is given by $y-y_{1}=m(x-x_{1})$

Since the line $PQ$ is passing through $(1,2)$ therefore its

equation is

$(y-2)=m(x-1)$

where $m$ is the slope of the line $PQ$ .

Now, point $P(x,0)$ will also satisfy the equation of $PQ$

$\therefore$ $y-2=m(x-1)$

$\Rightarrow 0-2=m(x-1)$

$\Rightarrow -2=m(x-1)$

$\Rightarrow x-1=\frac{-2}{m}$

$\Rightarrow x=\frac{-2}{m}+1$

Also, $OP=\sqrt{(x-0)^{2}+(0-0)^{2}}=x=\frac{-2}{m}+1$

Similarly, point $Q(0,y)$ will satisfy equation of $PQ$

$\therefore$ $y-2=m(x-1)$

$\Rightarrow y-2=m(-1) \Rightarrow y=2-m$ b

and $OQ=y=2-m$

Area of $\Delta POQ=\frac{1}{2}(OP)(OQ)=\frac{1}{2}(1-\frac{2}{m})(2-m)$

( As Area of $\Delta=\frac{1}{2} \times$ base $\times$ height )

$=\frac{1}{2}[2-m-\frac{4}{m}+2]=\frac{1}{2}[4-(m+\frac{4}{m})]$

$=2-\frac{m}{2}-\frac{2}{m}$



Let Area $=f(m)=2-\frac{m}{2}-\frac{2}{m}$

Now, $f^{'}(m)=\frac{-1}{2}+\frac{2}{m^{2}}$

Put $f^{'}(m)=0$

$\Rightarrow m^{2}=4 \Rightarrow m= \pm 2$

Now, $f^{''}(m)=\frac{-4}{m^{3}}$

$f^{''}(m)|_{m=2}=-\frac{1}{2}<0$

$f^{''}(m)|_{m=-2}=\frac{1}{2}>0$

Area will be least at $m=-2$

Hence, slope of $PQ$ is $-2.$

$\therefore$ $P(x)=x^{4}+ax^{3}+bx^{2}+d$

$\Rightarrow 1-a+b+d<1+a+b+d \Rightarrow a>0$

Now $P^{'}(x)=4x^{3}+3ax^{2}+2bx=x(4x^{2}+3ax+2b)$

As $P^{'}(x)=0,$ there is only one solution $x=0,$

therefore $4x^{2}+3ax+2b=0$ should not have any real roots i.e. $D<0$

$∀x>0$

Max $P(x)=P(1)$ and Min $P(x)=P(0)$

$\Rightarrow P(-1)$ is not minimum but $P(1)$ is the maximum of $P.$

questions.question_text: A lizard, at an initial distance of 21 cm behind an insect moves from rest with an acceleration of $2cm/s^{2}$ and pursues the insect which is crawling uniformly along a straight line at a speed of $20cm/s$ . Then the lizard will catch the insect after :
questions.question_html: A lizard, at an initial distance of 21 cm behind an insect moves from rest with an acceleration of $2cm/s^{2}$ and pursues the insect which is crawling uniformly along a straight line at a speed of $20cm/s$ . Then the lizard will catch the insect after :
questions.explanation_text: The motion of the lizard, which starts from rest and accelerates at a rate of $a=2\text{cm/s}^{2}$ , can be described by the equation of motion : $D_{l}=\frac{1}{2}at^{2}$ where $D_{l}$ is the distance the lizard travels, $a$ is its acceleration, and $t$ is the time. The insect, moving at a constant speed of $v=20\text{cm/s}$ , has a motion that can be simply described as: $D_{i}=vt$ where $D_{i}$ is the distance the insect travels, $v$ is its velocity, and $t$ is the time. Since the lizard starts 21 cm behind the insect and needs to catch up, it must travel the distance the insect travels plus an additional 21 cm. Equating these two distances gives us : $\frac{1}{2}at^{2}=vt+21$ Substituting the given values into this equation gives : $t^{2}=\frac{(vt+21) \cdot 2}{a}$ Substituting $a=2\text{cm/s}^{2}$ and $v=20\text{cm/s}$ , we simplify to : $t^{2}=20t+21$ This simplifies to a quadratic equation : $t^{2}-20t-21=0$ Solving this quadratic equation for $t$ gives the solutions $t=21\text{s}$ and $t=-1\text{s}$ . Since time cannot be negative, we discard the -1 s solution. Therefore, the lizard will catch the insect after 21 seconds. So, the correct answer is Option C : 21 s .
questions.explanation_html:
The motion of the lizard, which starts from rest and accelerates at a rate of $a=2\text{cm/s}^{2}$ , can be described by the equation of motion :

$D_{l}=\frac{1}{2}at^{2}$

where $D_{l}$ is the distance the lizard travels, $a$ is its acceleration, and $t$ is the time.

The insect, moving at a constant speed of $v=20\text{cm/s}$ , has a motion that can be simply described as:

$D_{i}=vt$

where $D_{i}$ is the distance the insect travels, $v$ is its velocity, and $t$ is the time.

Since the lizard starts 21 cm behind the insect and needs to catch up, it must travel the distance the insect travels plus an additional 21 cm. Equating these two distances gives us :

$\frac{1}{2}at^{2}=vt+21$

Substituting the given values into this equation gives :

$t^{2}=\frac{(vt+21) \cdot 2}{a}$

Substituting $a=2\text{cm/s}^{2}$ and $v=20\text{cm/s}$ , we simplify to :

$t^{2}=20t+21$

This simplifies to a quadratic equation :

$t^{2}-20t-21=0$

Solving this quadratic equation for $t$ gives the solutions $t=21\text{s}$ and $t=-1\text{s}$ . Since time cannot be negative, we discard the -1 s solution. Therefore, the lizard will catch the insect after 21 seconds.

So, the correct answer is Option C : 21 s.
